title: One giant durable pool of files built from thousands of dying servers
body: A distributed file system (DFS) is software that turns thousands of servers full of disks into one large, durable pool of files. A 1-billion-user app stores exabytes of photos and logs, far more than any single machine can hold, and any machine can die at any moment. So a DFS spreads each file across many machines, keeps enough redundancy to survive disk, host and rack failures, repairs itself, and gives programs a simple file path instead of a list of machines.
deeper:
The DFS sits at the bottom of almost every big company's storage stack. Higher layers such as databases, blob stores and analytics engines are built on top of it, so its behavior leaks upward into everything else.

The requirements hide in that one definition. Spreading files means the system must track where every piece lives. Redundancy means choosing between full copies (replication) and cheaper coded fragments (erasure coding). Self-repair means background processes must notice a dead disk and rebuild what it held without a human paging in. A simple path means clients must not need to know that a file is really scattered across dozens of servers in several racks.

Each of these duties generates bookkeeping. Knowing which bytes are where, which copies are stale, and which files exist is itself a large, fast-changing dataset. That bookkeeping, not the bytes themselves, turns out to be the hard part, and it is the thread that ties together every system covered in this chapter, from GFS in 2003 to Tectonic in 2021.

quiz.q: Why can't a large app simply store its files on a few very big servers?
quiz.a: No single machine can hold exabytes, and any machine can die at any moment, so data must be spread across many machines with redundancy and automatic repair.

title: Every DFS has two halves, and only one of them is hard
body: Every distributed file system splits into two parts. The data path stores and serves the actual bytes; it scales almost linearly, because adding storage servers adds capacity and throughput. The metadata path holds the namespace (directories and file names), the mapping from files to blocks, and the mapping from blocks to machines. The metadata path is the hard part: every open, create, list and rename touches it, and it must stay correct and consistent while the data path fans out across thousands of machines.
deeper:
Why does the data path scale so easily? Bytes of different files are independent. Two clients reading different blocks never need to coordinate, so you can add servers and spread the load without anyone talking to anyone else.

Metadata is different. The namespace is a single shared tree. Creating a file must check that the name does not already exist. Renaming a directory changes the path of everything under it. Listing a directory must see a consistent view. The block map must agree with what storage servers actually hold. These operations need coordination and ordering, and they are touched by every client on every file operation, even when the data itself is spread thinly.

Metadata also grows with the number of files, not the number of bytes. A cluster holding a billion small files needs a billion namespace entries even if the total data is modest. That is why the most important question in reviewing any storage system is where the metadata lives and how it grows. Many outages that look like data outages are really metadata outages, a theme the chapter returns to repeatedly.

quiz.q: Why does the data path of a DFS scale almost linearly while the metadata path does not?
quiz.a: Bytes of different files are independent, so adding servers adds throughput. Metadata is a shared, ordered structure every operation touches, and it grows with file count.

title: Two decades of DFS designs, one question: how do we scale metadata?
body: The main story of distributed file systems is that every generation is a new answer to one question: how do we scale metadata? GFS put all metadata in the RAM of one machine. HDFS copied that design, then added federation (several masters) and read replicas. Colossus and Tectonic moved metadata into a distributed database. Ceph removed part of the metadata entirely by computing data placement with a formula instead of storing it in a table.
deeper:
This framing turns a zoo of systems into a progression. Each approach solves the previous one's bottleneck and introduces its own.

One in-memory master (GFS, early HDFS) gives simple code and strong metadata semantics but runs out of RAM, CPU and recovery time. Federation splits the tree across masters but leaves hot directories hot. Read replicas offload the majority of operations, which are reads, yet writes still hit one node. A distributed database (Bigtable under Colossus, ZippyDB under Tectonic) scales to billions of files but makes cross-shard operations such as rename hard. Computed placement (Ceph's CRUSH) has no block-location table at all, but data moves whenever the cluster map changes.

The data path barely changes across these generations: clients still find out where bytes live and then talk directly to storage servers. What changes is who knows where the bytes live, and how that knowledge is stored, partitioned and recovered. Reading each system through this lens makes it easy to predict its limits before reading its failure stories.

quiz.q: What single design question do GFS, HDFS, Colossus, Tectonic and Ceph each answer differently?
quiz.a: How to scale metadata: one RAM master, federated masters plus read replicas, a distributed database, or computing placement with a formula instead of storing it.

title: GFS was built on the assumption that hardware always fails
body: The Google File System paper (SOSP 2003) started from assumptions that were unusual at the time. Component failures are the norm on cheap commodity machines. Files are huge. Most writes are appends and most reads are large streams. Sustained bandwidth matters more than latency. And many clients may append to the same file at once. These fit Google's early crawl, indexing and MapReduce workloads, and they explain every design choice GFS made.
deeper:
The chapter stresses that these assumptions were unusual at the time. Designing for failure as the norm means detection and automatic repair must be built in, not bolted on.

Each assumption maps to a design choice. Huge files justify huge 64 MB chunks. Append-heavy writes justify a special record append operation rather than optimizing random overwrites. Streaming reads and a bandwidth focus justify pushing data along chains of servers to use full network bandwidth, even at some cost in latency. Many concurrent appenders justify relaxed consistency, where GFS picks the offset and applications handle duplicates.

The flip side is that the design fits its original workload very well and other workloads poorly. When Google later needed latency-sensitive services and billions of small files, the same assumptions became liabilities. A good lesson from GFS is to write down your workload assumptions explicitly, because they silently decide what your system will be bad at later.

quiz.q: Why did GFS favor sustained bandwidth over low latency?
quiz.a: Its workloads (crawl, indexing, MapReduce) were large streaming reads and appends, so throughput mattered most; latency-sensitive services were not the target.

title: GFS architecture: one master, many chunkservers, 64 MB chunks
body: A GFS cluster has one master and many chunkservers, accessed by many clients. Files are split into fixed-size chunks of 64 MB, each with a globally unique 64-bit chunk handle. Chunkservers store chunks as ordinary Linux files on local disks, and each chunk is replicated on 3 chunkservers by default. The master holds all metadata; the chunkservers hold all the bytes. Clients link a GFS client library into their application to talk to both.
deeper:
The division of labor is sharp. The master knows the namespace, which chunks make up each file, and where each chunk's replicas are. Chunkservers know nothing about files or directories; they just store chunk-sized Linux files keyed by handle and answer reads and writes.

A read works in three steps. The client library converts a file name and byte offset into a chunk index and asks the master. The master replies with the chunk handle and replica locations. The client then reads or writes data directly with a chunkserver. The master also exchanges heartbeats and instructions with chunkservers, which is how it learns their state and tells them to re-replicate or delete chunks.

Storing chunks as plain Linux files was a pragmatic choice: the local file system handles space allocation and disk layout, and GFS only adds distribution, replication and naming on top. Three-way replication on cheap machines gave durability without specialized hardware, fitting the assumption that failures are constant. The single master made the design simple to build and reason about, and would later become its main limit.

quiz.q: In GFS, what does a chunkserver know about files and directories?
quiz.a: Nothing. It stores chunks as Linux files keyed by 64-bit handle; the master alone knows the namespace and the file-to-chunk mapping.

title: The GFS master keeps everything in RAM, backed by an operation log
body: The GFS master holds all metadata in memory: the namespace, the mapping from files to chunks, and the location of each chunk's replicas. It keeps less than 64 bytes of metadata per 64 MB chunk. Keeping everything in RAM makes metadata operations fast and lets the master scan its whole state for background work. Durability comes from an operation log: namespace changes are written to it and replicated to remote machines, with periodic checkpoints so recovery is fast.
deeper:
The operation log is the master's source of durability. A namespace change is not acknowledged until the log record is safely written locally and on remote replicas, so a crash cannot lose a completed operation.

Checkpoints keep recovery bounded. Replaying years of log records from the beginning would be too slow, so the master periodically writes a compact snapshot of its state. On restart it loads the latest checkpoint and replays only the log records written after it.

The tiny per-chunk footprint is what made one master viable. At under 64 bytes per 64 MB chunk, a petabyte of data costs about 1 GB of master RAM for chunk metadata. But recovery still takes real time: load the checkpoint, replay the log, and during that window writes stop. That recovery time, along with RAM for file names and the CPU of one machine, became part of the reason GFS eventually hit a ceiling. The design choice is a classic one: simplicity and speed now, with a known limit later.

quiz.q: How does the GFS master stay durable when all its metadata lives in RAM?
quiz.a: Namespace changes go to an operation log replicated on remote machines, with periodic checkpoints so recovery loads a snapshot and replays only recent records.

title: Why the GFS master never writes down where chunks live
body: The GFS master does not persist chunk locations. Instead it learns them from chunkservers at startup and through regular heartbeats. The chunkserver is treated as the source of truth for which chunks it holds, so the master never drifts out of sync with reality. Disks fail, chunkservers restart, and machines get renamed or added; rather than keep a stored list consistent with all that churn, the master simply asks.
deeper:
This is a subtle and influential choice. If the master persisted chunk locations, every disk failure, machine replacement and chunkserver restart would need a coordinated update, and any missed update would leave the master believing a replica exists when it does not. In a cluster with constant failures, that disagreement would be common.

By polling instead, the master's view is always rebuilt from what the chunkservers actually report. At startup it collects reports from every chunkserver; afterwards, heartbeats keep the picture current. The persisted state (namespace and file-to-chunk mapping, via the operation log) covers only what the master alone decides.

HDFS copied this idea directly: DataNodes send block reports to the NameNode. The trade-off appears at scale. Block reports from thousands of nodes are themselves a large RPC load on one process, one of the reasons HDFS NameNodes later struggled with RPC throughput. Still, the principle holds widely: let the component that physically owns a fact be the authority for it.

quiz.q: Why does the GFS master not persist chunk replica locations?
quiz.a: Chunkservers are the source of truth; with constant failures, a stored list would drift. Rebuilding locations from startup reports and heartbeats keeps the master in sync.

title: GFS clients never read file data through the master
body: In GFS, clients never read file data through the master. They ask the master where a chunk lives, cache the answer, and then talk directly to chunkservers for the actual bytes. The master handles only small metadata requests. This keeps the single master from becoming a data bottleneck: its CPU and network card serve tiny lookups while the heavy traffic spreads across thousands of chunkservers.
deeper:
Separating the lookup from the transfer is the pattern every system in this chapter reuses. Colossus clients talk to curators for control operations and read directly from D file servers. HDFS clients get block locations from the NameNode and stream from DataNodes. Lustre clients get a layout from the metadata target and read many object storage targets directly.

Client caching multiplies the benefit. Because a chunk's location rarely changes, a client can reuse the answer for many reads and skip the master entirely.

The limit is that caching helps only once a client knows about a file. Opening, creating, listing and deleting files still go to the master. When thousands of MapReduce tasks start at once and each opens files, those metadata calls pile up at one machine. So keeping data off the master was necessary but not sufficient: metadata operation rate itself eventually became the bottleneck.

quiz.q: How does GFS stop its single master from becoming a data bottleneck?
quiz.a: The master only answers small location lookups, which clients cache; all file bytes flow directly between clients and chunkservers.

title: Why GFS picked huge 64 MB chunks, and the hot-spot cost
body: GFS used 64 MB chunks, huge by file system standards. Fewer chunks mean less master RAM and fewer client-to-master calls, since one lookup covers a big range of a file. The cost falls on small files: a small file is just one chunk, stored on only a few chunkservers. If many readers hit it at once, those few machines become hot spots. The GFS paper describes exactly this with an executable stored in GFS and started on hundreds of machines at once.
deeper:
The arithmetic behind big chunks is simple: master memory and lookup traffic scale with the number of chunks, so a larger chunk size directly shrinks both. With 64 MB chunks and under 64 bytes of metadata each, a petabyte needs about 16 million chunks and roughly 1 GB of master RAM.

The hot-spot problem is a mismatch between chunk granularity and access pattern. A popular large file spreads its load over many chunks and therefore many servers. A popular small file cannot: all readers converge on the handful of replicas holding its single chunk. With hundreds of machines launching the same executable simultaneously, the few chunkservers holding it became hot spots.

Later systems shifted the default: HDFS uses 128 MB blocks, while Azure packs many small objects into 1 GB extents and keeps a separate index for them. Chunk size is always a trade between metadata cost and load spreading for small, popular objects.

quiz.q: What is the downside of GFS's large 64 MB chunk size for small files?
quiz.a: A small file is one chunk on only a few chunkservers, so many simultaneous readers turn those servers into hot spots.

title: Leases: how GFS makes 3 replicas apply writes in the same order
body: With 3 replicas, GFS must ensure every replica applies writes in the same order. It uses leases. The master grants a chunk lease to one replica, called the primary. The lease has an initial timeout of 60 seconds and can be extended while writes continue. The primary picks a serial order for all writes to that chunk, and the other replicas, called secondaries, apply writes in exactly that order. The master is involved only in granting leases, not in each write.
deeper:
A lease is a time-limited grant of authority. While the primary holds it, only that replica decides mutation order, so there is never a conflict between replicas about which write came first.

The timeout is what makes leases safe under failure. If the primary crashes or becomes unreachable, the master does not need to contact it; it just waits for the lease to expire and then grants a new lease to another replica. There can never be two primaries at once, because the old lease must run out before a new one is issued. Extensions keep a busy chunk's primary stable while writes continue.

This design moves per-write ordering off the master. The master's job shrinks to granting and extending leases for actively written chunks, while the primaries handle the high-frequency ordering work. It is an early, widely copied example of using time-bounded delegation to scale coordination: centralize the rare decision (who is in charge), distribute the frequent one (what order).

quiz.q: Why does a GFS lease have a timeout instead of lasting until revoked?
quiz.a: If the primary fails, the master just waits for the lease to expire and grants a new one, never risking two primaries and never needing the dead primary's cooperation.

title: GFS pushes data along a chain, then sends the write command
body: GFS separates data flow from control flow. The client first pushes the data along a chain of chunkservers, each forwarding to the next closest one, to use every machine's full network bandwidth. Only after all replicas have the data does the client send the write request to the primary. The primary assigns a serial number, applies the write, and tells the secondaries to apply it in that serial order. They report done to the primary, which returns success or an error to the client.
deeper:
The full sequence: the client asks the master who holds the lease for the chunk, and gets primary and secondary locations. It pushes the data to the nearest replica, which forwards along the chain to the others. Then the control message goes to the primary, which orders and applies it and instructs secondaries.

Why a chain instead of the client sending to all three? If the client sent three copies, its outbound link would be split three ways. In a chain, each machine uses its full outbound bandwidth to forward to the next, so the transfer takes about as long as sending one copy, plus small pipeline delays. Choosing the next closest machine minimizes cross-rack traffic.

Decoupling means the network-heavy part can follow whatever path is best for bandwidth, while the ordering decision stays with the primary regardless of network topology. The same idea of splitting bulk data movement from small coordination messages appears again and again in storage systems: Colossus, Tectonic and HDFS all keep bytes and control on separate paths.

quiz.q: Why does GFS forward data along a chain of chunkservers instead of having the client send to every replica?
quiz.a: Each machine uses its full outbound bandwidth forwarding to the next closest one, so replicating costs about one transfer, instead of the client's link being split three ways.

title: Chunk version numbers catch replicas that missed writes
body: A stale replica is one that missed writes while its chunkserver was down. GFS detects them with a chunk version number. The master keeps a version number for each chunk and increases it every time it grants a new lease. Up-to-date replicas record the new version. When a chunkserver comes back and reports its chunks, any replica with an older version is known to be stale and can be excluded and garbage-collected.
deeper:
The trick is tying the version bump to lease grants. A new lease means a new round of mutations is about to begin, so every replica that participates learns the new number. A replica on a machine that was down at that moment keeps the old number.

Because chunkservers report their chunks and versions at startup and in heartbeats, the master can compare each reported version against its own record. Stale replicas are never handed to clients as valid locations, and the system re-replicates from good copies to restore the replication factor.

This matters because the master learns chunk locations from chunkservers rather than persisting them. Without versions, a returning chunkserver's report would look indistinguishable from a healthy replica, and clients might read old data. A single monotonic counter per chunk, incremented at the natural boundary of a new lease, cheaply closes that gap. Versioning or epoch numbers of this kind are a standard tool for rejecting state from a participant that was absent during a change.

quiz.q: Why does GFS bump a chunk's version number when it grants a new lease?
quiz.a: Replicas present for the lease learn the new version; a replica that was down keeps the old one, so on return its lower version exposes it as stale.

title: Record append: GFS picks the offset, and appends at least once
body: GFS added a special operation called record append. The client supplies only the data, not the offset. GFS appends it atomically at least once, at an offset GFS chooses, and returns that offset. Many producers can append to one file with no locking between them. The catch is 'at least once': if an append fails on one replica, the client retries, and the retry lands at a new offset. Some replicas may then contain the record twice, or padding or partial garbage in the failed region.
deeper:
Record append fits workloads like many MapReduce workers writing results into one output file, or a file used as a producer-consumer queue. With ordinary writes, each producer would need to agree on offsets, requiring distributed locking. Letting the primary choose the offset removes that coordination.

The primary, which already orders all writes to the chunk, chooses the offset and the secondaries follow it.

Failure is where semantics get loose. If one secondary fails, the client sees an error and retries the whole append. The replicas that already wrote the first attempt keep it, so after the retry succeeds, those replicas hold the record twice, while the failed replica has garbage or padding at that range. GFS guarantees the record appears as one contiguous unit at least once at the same offset on all replicas, but not that the file is byte-identical across replicas. Handling the leftovers was left to applications.

quiz.q: How can a successful GFS record append leave a duplicate record on some replicas?
quiz.a: If the append fails on one replica, the client retries; replicas that wrote the first attempt keep it, and the retry lands at a new offset, so they hold it twice.

title: GFS consistency in two words: consistent vs defined
body: GFS defines its consistency model with two words. A file region is consistent if all clients see the same data, no matter which replica they read. A region is defined if it is consistent and clients see exactly what one mutation wrote. Successful serial writes leave a region defined. Concurrent successful writes leave it consistent but undefined, with mixed fragments from several writers. A failed write leaves it inconsistent. Record append gives defined records, possibly with inconsistent regions between them.
deeper:
These definitions separate two questions: do replicas agree, and does the content make sense as one writer's output?

Consider two clients overwriting the same large range concurrently. Their writes may be split into chunk-sized operations, and the primary may interleave pieces from both. Every replica applies the same interleaving, so all readers see the same bytes (consistent), but those bytes are a patchwork no single client wrote (undefined).

A failed write is worse: some replicas applied it and some did not, so readers can get different answers depending on which replica they hit (inconsistent).

Record append sits in between. Each successfully appended record is defined, an intact copy of what one client wrote, but the regions around it may contain padding, fragments of failed attempts, or duplicates that differ across replicas. This vocabulary is useful beyond GFS because it makes explicit what many storage systems leave vague: replica agreement and write atomicity are different guarantees, and a system can offer one without the other.

quiz.q: What state do concurrent successful overwrites leave a GFS region in, and why?
quiz.a: Consistent but undefined: all replicas apply the same interleaving, so readers agree, but the bytes mix fragments from several writers.

title: GFS pushed part of correctness onto every application
body: GFS's relaxed consistency meant applications had to clean up after it. The paper says applications use checksums to skip padding and fragments, and unique record IDs to drop duplicates created by at-least-once record append. In other words, GFS pushed part of the correctness burden up to the application. That was acceptable when the users were batch jobs written by a few teams at Google. It became painful later, as more teams and more kinds of applications built on GFS.
deeper:
The approach works through self-validating records. A writer includes a checksum with each record, so a reader scanning the file can recognize padding and partial garbage as invalid and skip it. Each record also carries a unique ID, so a reader that encounters the same ID twice can discard the repeat.

The trade-off is organizational as much as technical. Relaxing consistency made the file system simpler and faster at concurrent appends. But every consumer now had to know about duplicates and garbage regions, and any application that forgot, or that needed strict semantics, got subtle bugs.

Later this was listed among the reasons GFS hit its limits: relaxed consistency leaked into every application. The newer systems in this chapter, such as Azure's stream layer designed with strong consistency from the start, and Tectonic's single writer per file with linearizable metadata, reflect that lesson. Weak guarantees at the bottom of the stack get paid for many times over at the top.

quiz.q: How do GFS applications cope with duplicates and garbage from record append?
quiz.a: Records carry checksums so readers skip padding and fragments, and unique IDs so readers drop duplicates, pushing part of correctness into the application.

title: GFS extras: lazy deletion, shadow masters, and a 15-minute wait
body: GFS had several other good ideas. Deletion was lazy: files were removed through background garbage collection instead of immediately. Read-only shadow masters served reads when the master was down. Copy-on-write snapshots made fast file and directory copies. And GFS used delayed recovery: it typically waited 15 minutes before re-replicating chunks from an unavailable node, because most unavailability is short. By 2003 the largest GFS clusters had over 1,000 storage nodes, over 300 TB of disk, and hundreds of clients.
deeper:
Each extra trades immediacy for robustness. Lazy deletion lets a batched background process reclaim space, which is simpler than synchronously deleting replicas across many machines and gives a window to recover from mistakes.

Shadow masters follow the operation log and provide read-only access, keeping reads available during a master outage, though possibly slightly behind.

Copy-on-write snapshots avoid copying data up front: the snapshot and the original share chunks until one of them is modified, and only then is a new chunk created.

Delayed recovery is reported in the 2010 Google OSDI availability study, which notes that GFS typically waited 15 minutes. Most nodes that disappear come back quickly after a reboot or a brief network problem. Re-replicating immediately would move huge amounts of data for nothing and consume disk and network bandwidth needed by real traffic. Waiting 15 minutes filters out transient blips while still repairing real failures promptly.

For scale context, 1,000+ nodes and 300+ TB was large in 2003. Colossus would later scale over 100x beyond the largest GFS clusters.

quiz.q: Why did GFS wait about 15 minutes before re-replicating chunks from an unavailable node?
quiz.a: Most unavailability is short; immediate re-replication would waste disk and network moving data for nodes that soon return.

title: Why GFS hit its limits: file count, not bytes
body: The single master was both a brilliant simplification and the ceiling. At under 64 bytes per 64 MB chunk, 1 PB is about 16 million chunks and about 1 GB of master RAM, which looks fine. But file count, not bytes, is the real limit: a billion small files means a billion namespace entries in one machine's RAM. One master also means one CPU and one NIC for every metadata operation, so thousands of MapReduce tasks opening files at once turn it into a queue.
deeper:
The full list of limits has five parts. First, file count: namespace entries grow with the number of files regardless of their size. Second, one CPU and one network card serve all metadata operations, creating a queue under bursty load. Third, 64 MB chunks and a batch-oriented design do not fit latency-sensitive services. Fourth, master recovery takes time: load the checkpoint, replay the log, and meanwhile writes stop. Fifth, relaxed consistency leaked into every application.

The back-of-envelope number (1 GB of RAM per PB for chunk metadata) is deceptive because it assumes large files. Workloads shift toward many small files, and each file pays a fixed namespace cost. RAM, CPU and recovery time are the three metadata resources, and any of them can run out first.

A useful habit from this analysis is to label assumptions in capacity math. The chunk figure came straight from the paper; the danger lay in the unstated assumption about file sizes. Changing that one assumption turns a comfortable design into one that fails.

quiz.q: Why can a GFS-style master run out of RAM even when total data is modest?
quiz.a: Namespace entries grow with file count, not bytes; a billion small files means a billion entries in one machine's RAM regardless of total size.

title: Google's own account: GFS outgrew one master, so came Colossus
body: In a 2009 ACM Queue interview, GFS tech lead Sean Quinlan described the pains of GFS at scale: file counts growing on a single master, the move to running multiple GFS cells and masters, the poor fit for latency-sensitive applications, and work on a new design with distributed masters. Google's 2021 Colossus blog post confirms the result: Colossus was built to fix GFS's metadata scaling limits. The single-master design had carried Google far, but it could not carry it further.
deeper:
The interview is valuable because it is an insider's post-mortem on a successful system. The workarounds it describes are typical of a design reaching its ceiling.

Running multiple cells, each with its own master, is a form of static partitioning. It buys headroom but pushes complexity onto users, who must know which cell holds their data, and it does not help a single hot namespace.

The latency problem came from new workloads. GFS was designed for batch jobs where a master failover or a slow chunk transfer mattered little. Serving latency-sensitive applications on top of it exposed master recovery time and the batch-oriented chunk design.

The eventual fix went to the root: distribute the masters. Colossus put metadata into Bigtable behind horizontally scaled curators, so metadata was no longer limited to one machine's RAM. This arc, a simple central design followed by partitioning workarounds and then a redesign with distributed metadata, repeats in HDFS and at Meta, and is worth recognizing early in any system you run.

quiz.q: What stopgap did Google use before Colossus to get around GFS's single master?
quiz.a: Running multiple GFS cells, each with its own master, which added headroom but did not fix per-master limits or latency-sensitive workloads.

title: A single master isn't the mistake; having no exit plan is
body: Senior staff lens: a single master is not a mistake for a young system. It gives simple code and strong metadata semantics, and it lets a small team ship. The real mistake is having no plan for outgrowing it. For any centralized metadata design, ask which metadata resource runs out first, RAM, CPU, or recovery time, and when. Knowing the answer lets you schedule the redesign before the ceiling becomes an outage.
deeper:
Each resource has a different growth driver. RAM tracks file and block count. CPU tracks metadata operations per second, which spikes with batch job launches and listing-heavy workloads. Recovery time tracks the size of checkpoint plus log to replay, and it grows quietly until one failover takes long enough to breach an availability target.

A practical plan tracks all three against capacity, and projects the date each would cross a threshold. It also identifies the likely escape routes in advance: federation, read replicas, moving metadata into a distributed database, or restructuring data into fewer, larger objects. The HDFS community followed the incremental route with federation, high availability and observers. Google took the redesign route with Colossus.

The broader lesson is that architectural simplicity is a loan. Early on it is cheap and fast. The interest comes due as growth continues, and teams that monitor the specific resource that will run out can refinance on their own schedule instead of during an incident.

quiz.q: For a single-master metadata design, which three resources should you track to know when it will run out?
quiz.a: RAM (grows with file and block count), CPU (grows with metadata operation rate), and recovery time (grows with checkpoint plus log size).

title: Colossus: what Google has actually published
body: Google has never published a full Colossus paper. What is known comes from Google Cloud blog posts in 2021 and 2025, and from research papers that mention it. Anything beyond these sources should be treated as speculation. The April 2021 post 'A peek behind Colossus' describes the components: a client library, curators, a metadata database in Bigtable, D file servers, and custodians. The most complex piece is the client library, which talks to the rest of Colossus on the application's behalf.
deeper:
The client library implements software RAID and chooses among different encodings, replication or erasure codes, to trade performance against cost. That means encoding happens on the client side, not in the storage servers. The client library decides how a file's data is split and protected, then writes fragments directly to storage.

Pushing complexity into the client has consequences. It lets each application pick encodings suited to its workload, and it keeps storage servers simple. But it makes the client library the component that must be correct and carefully upgraded, since bugs there affect data layout for everyone using it.

The discipline about sources matters because Colossus is widely discussed and frequently described with invented detail. The chapter explicitly flags that Google has not published how the recursion bottoms out, since Bigtable itself stores data on a file system. When reasoning about Colossus, stick to what the 2021 and 2025 posts and the related research papers say, and label anything else as a guess.

quiz.q: Where does encoding (replication vs erasure coding) happen in Colossus?
quiz.a: In the client library, which implements software RAID and picks an encoding per use to trade performance against cost.

title: Curators plus Bigtable: metadata escapes one machine's RAM
body: Colossus replaces GFS's single master with curators, a scalable control plane. Clients talk to curators for control operations like creating, opening or deleting a file, and curators scale horizontally. Curators store file system metadata in Bigtable, Google's distributed database. This is the key change from GFS: metadata is no longer limited to one machine's RAM. Google says storing metadata in Bigtable let Colossus scale over 100x beyond the largest GFS clusters, to exabytes and tens of thousands of machines in one cluster.
deeper:
The durable metadata lives in Bigtable rows, not in curator memory. Adding curators adds metadata operation capacity, and Bigtable shards the metadata across many servers, so neither RAM, CPU nor a single recovery log caps the system the way the GFS master did.

This is the 'metadata in a distributed database' approach. Its strengths are scale to billions of files and exabytes. Its standard weakness is cross-shard operations: anything that must change several rows atomically across partitions, such as a rename, becomes harder than in a single process.

It also creates a curious recursion. Bigtable stores its own data on a file system, and at Google that file system is Colossus. The chain must bottom out in something smaller and simpler that does not depend on Colossus-scale metadata. Google has not published how this works, so claims you read online about it deserve caution. Tectonic later repeated the same pattern using ZippyDB.

quiz.q: What was the key change from GFS that let Colossus scale over 100x?
quiz.a: Metadata moved from one master's RAM into Bigtable, served by horizontally scaled curators.

title: D servers hold the bytes; custodians keep them alive
body: Colossus stores data on D file servers, which are network-attached disks. Data flows directly between clients and D servers with minimal network hops, keeping the curators out of the data path. Background services called custodians keep data durable and available: they rebalance disk space across servers and run RAID reconstruction, which rebuilds lost fragments after a disk or server fails. Together with client-side encoding, this makes storage servers simple and puts intelligence in the client and background services.
deeper:
The D servers are deliberately thin. Because the client library already decided the encoding and computed fragments, D servers just store and serve bytes, on HDD or SSD. Minimal hops matter for latency: a read goes from client to disk server with nothing in between.

Custodians are the self-repair half of the system. In a cluster of tens of thousands of machines, disks fail constantly. With erasure coding, a lost fragment must be rebuilt by reading surviving fragments and recomputing the missing one, which is the RAID reconstruction the 2021 post describes. Rebalancing moves data when new disks arrive or some fill up, so capacity and load stay even.

A similar pattern shows up across the chapter: GFS's master directed re-replication, Tectonic has background services for garbage collection, repair, rebalancing and rack drains, and HDFS DataNodes are directed by the NameNode. Colossus splits these duties into dedicated services rather than burdening the control plane or storage servers, so repair can scale separately from metadata operations.

quiz.q: What do Colossus custodians do?
quiz.a: Background work for durability and availability: rebalancing disk space and running RAID reconstruction to rebuild lost fragments.

title: How Google moved from 3x replication to Reed-Solomon
body: A 2010 Google OSDI paper on availability, written by the storage team, modeled replication and Reed-Solomon (RS) encodings in Google's storage cells. The cells it validated against used mostly RS(5,3) and 3x replication at the time, and it discussed multi-cell schemes like RS(6,3) in each of three cells. It says its analysis influenced the design of Google's 'next generation distributed storage system'. Combined with client-side software RAID described in 2021, the picture is that Colossus moved much of Google's data from 3x replication to Reed-Solomon, with the client encoding.
deeper:
Reed-Solomon codes split data into data fragments and add parity fragments so that the original can be rebuilt from a subset of them. They cost far less space than keeping three full copies, at the price of more work to rebuild a lost fragment and more complex writes.

The same 2010 paper is also the source for GFS's delayed recovery: it reports that GFS typically waited 15 minutes before re-replicating, since most unavailability is short.

Note how the chapter builds its conclusion from two published sources rather than asserting it outright: the OSDI paper describes encodings in use and its influence on the next generation system, and the 2021 Colossus post describes client-side software RAID choosing between replication and erasure codes. Together they support the conclusion. This is a model for reasoning about systems whose designs are only partly public: connect documented facts and label the inference.

quiz.q: What two published sources together support the claim that Colossus moved much data to Reed-Solomon?
quiz.a: The 2010 OSDI availability paper (RS encodings, influence on the next-gen system) and the 2021 Colossus post (client-side software RAID choosing encodings).

title: Colossus in 2025: two file systems over 10 EB each
body: In March 2025, Google said many Colossus file systems hold multiple exabytes and two exceed 10 EB each. Throughput regularly exceeds 50 TB/s read and 25 TB/s write, and the busiest cluster serves over 600 million IOPS. There is one zonal Colossus file system per cluster, and it is append-only. An SSD cache called L4, guided by an ML-based policy, decides which data lives on SSD versus HDD, so hot data gets flash speed while most bytes stay on cheaper disks.
deeper:
These numbers show how far the metadata-in-a-database design has carried: a single file system of more than 10 EB would be unthinkable with a GFS-style single master.

Append-only is a notable constraint. Like Azure's stream layer and Tectonic, Colossus does not support arbitrary overwrites. Append-only data simplifies replication, encoding and caching, because written bytes never change, and higher layers such as Bigtable and Spanner are designed around it.

The L4 cache addresses the economics of disks. HDDs are cheap per byte but offer few operations per second. Placing all data on SSD would be expensive, while leaving hot data on HDD would bottleneck on IOPS. L4 index servers track what is cached; the client library checks for a cache hit or miss before going to D servers. The ML-based policy decides placement dynamically instead of relying on manual tiering rules.

quiz.q: Why does Colossus use an SSD cache (L4) instead of putting all data on SSD or all on HDD?
quiz.a: All-SSD is too expensive and all-HDD bottlenecks on IOPS; L4 with an ML policy puts hot data on SSD and keeps most bytes on cheap disks.

title: Colossus's stateful protocol: sub-millisecond durable appends
body: In April 2025, Google described Colossus's stateful protocol. When a client opens a file, it gets a handle containing the data's disk locations, then talks to disks directly over an RDMA-like protocol. Durable appends reach sub-millisecond latency by writing to several disks in parallel and acknowledging once a quorum has the data. Spanner, Bigtable and BigQuery use this protocol, and it now powers Cloud Storage Rapid Storage, which supports up to 20 million requests per second in one bucket.
deeper:
'Stateful' means the client holds a session with location information obtained at open time, instead of looking up locations on every request. Subsequent operations skip metadata lookups entirely and go straight to disks.

RDMA-like access minimizes CPU and software overhead on the path between client and disk, which matters when targeting sub-millisecond latency.

Quorum writes cut tail latency: rather than waiting for every replica, the append is durable once enough disks confirm it, so one slow disk does not delay the whole write. Tectonic's blob storage uses the same idea with quorum appends and hedged writes.

This shows how far Colossus moved from GFS's batch assumptions. GFS was explicitly designed for bandwidth over latency, and its poor fit for latency-sensitive applications was one of its documented pains. Colossus now underpins Google's databases and a user-facing product that needs very high request rates with low latency. The same file system serves both huge throughput and fast small appends, an ambition GFS never had.

quiz.q: How does Colossus's stateful protocol achieve sub-millisecond durable appends?
quiz.a: The client gets disk locations at open, talks to disks directly over an RDMA-like protocol, and writes to several disks in parallel, acknowledging on a quorum.

title: Metadata in a database that itself lives on the file system
body: In industry: Colossus shows a pattern Tectonic repeats. Put file system metadata in a scalable database, even though that database stores its own data on a file system. Colossus keeps metadata in Bigtable, and Bigtable stores its data on Colossus. The recursion must bottom out in something smaller and simpler, which can bootstrap without depending on the big system. Google has not published those details, so be careful with claims you read online about how it works.
deeper:
The recursion works because each level is much smaller than the one above. File system metadata is a tiny fraction of the file system's data. The metadata of the database's own storage is a tiny fraction of that. After a few levels, what remains is small enough for a simple system to handle. What that base layer is at Google has not been published, so any specific answer is a guess.

Tectonic follows the same approach: its Name, File and Block layers live in ZippyDB, Meta's sharded key-value store. JuiceFS packages the idea for anyone: metadata in an engine like Redis or TiKV, data in an object store.

The operational danger of recursion is circular dependency during recovery. If the database needs the file system to start, and the file system needs the database to serve metadata, a full outage could deadlock unless the base layer is independent. That is why the bottom layer must be simpler and self-sufficient. When evaluating such designs, always ask what the base of the stack is and how it restarts from cold.

quiz.q: Why must the Colossus-Bigtable recursion bottom out in something smaller and simpler?
quiz.a: Bigtable stores data on Colossus, which stores metadata in Bigtable; a small, independent base layer is needed to avoid circular dependency and bootstrap from cold.

title: HDFS: GFS rebuilt in open source, almost one-to-one
body: The Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) began as an open-source system modeled on GFS and powered the Hadoop era at Yahoo, Facebook, LinkedIn, Uber, Twitter and thousands of other companies. The NameNode is the single metadata server: it keeps the full namespace and block map in RAM, persists the namespace in a file called the FsImage, and logs every change to the EditLog. DataNodes store blocks, typically 128 MB each. It maps almost one-to-one: NameNode = master, DataNode = chunkserver, block = chunk.
deeper:
The FsImage and EditLog mirror GFS's checkpoint and operation log. The FsImage is a snapshot of the namespace; the EditLog records every change since. On restart, the NameNode loads the FsImage and replays the EditLog.

DataNodes send heartbeats and block reports (the list of blocks they hold) to the NameNode, just as GFS chunkservers reported chunks. The NameNode therefore learns block locations from the DataNodes rather than trusting stored data.

Files are write-once-read-many: written once, with support for append and truncate but not arbitrary overwrites. That matches the batch analytics workloads Hadoop targeted.

The 128 MB block size, double GFS's 64 MB, reduces NameNode memory per byte stored, since memory scales with objects.

Because HDFS copied the GFS architecture, it also inherited GFS's ceiling: all metadata in one process's memory and all metadata operations through one server. Much of HDFS's later history, federation, high availability, observers, is a series of additions pushing against that single-master limit.

quiz.q: How does HDFS's FsImage and EditLog correspond to GFS?
quiz.a: FsImage is the namespace checkpoint and EditLog the operation log; on restart the NameNode loads the FsImage and replays the EditLog, as the GFS master did.

title: Rack-aware placement: survive a rack loss, cross racks only once
body: HDFS places 3 replicas with rack awareness. The first replica goes on the writer's node (or a random node in the writer's rack). The second goes on a node in a different rack. The third goes on a different node in that same remote rack. This layout survives the loss of an entire rack, since two racks each hold at least one copy, while crossing between racks only once per write, which saves scarce cross-rack network bandwidth.
deeper:
The write pipeline follows the GFS chain idea: the client sends data to the first DataNode, which forwards to the second, which forwards to the third. With this placement, only the hop from the first to the second node crosses racks. The hop from the second to the third stays inside the remote rack.

Placing each replica in a different rack would add a second cross-rack hop to every write. The chosen layout already survives the loss of any one rack, so it gets rack-level durability at the lowest cross-rack cost.

Why put the first copy on the writer's node (or its rack)? The first hop then stays local, so only one hop in the pipeline crosses racks.

This is the failure-domain thinking from earlier storage design applied to a concrete policy. Ceph later expresses the same idea as a CRUSH rule, such as '3 replicas in 3 different racks', computed by a function instead of chosen by a central server.

quiz.q: Why does HDFS put the second and third replicas in the same remote rack instead of in two different racks?
quiz.a: It still survives a full rack failure, but crosses racks only once per write, saving cross-rack bandwidth; two simultaneous rack failures are rare.

title: The NameNode memory limit: about 600 bytes per file
body: Konstantin Shvachko, then at Yahoo, did the NameNode math in 2010. A NameNode uses fewer than 200 bytes per metadata object, where an object is a file or a block. An average file had 1.5 blocks, so it cost about 600 bytes: one file object plus two block objects. At that rate, 100 million files need at least 60 GB of NameNode RAM. His rule of thumb: 1 GB of metadata is roughly 1 PB of physical storage.
deeper:
The math generalizes. 500 million average files need about 600 bytes times 500 million, or around 300 GB of RAM, in the same range as LinkedIn's later 380 GB NameNode heap holding about 1 billion objects.

Note that the 600-byte figure counts 2 block objects per file even though the average is 1.5 blocks, so it rounds up and errs on the generous side (3 objects x 200 bytes).

The rule of 1 GB of metadata per PB holds only for typical file sizes. A workload of tiny files blows it up, because each file pays the object cost regardless of its size. That is why small files are a capacity problem for HDFS, not just a performance problem.

Shvachko also reported node failure rates of 2 to 3 per 1,000 nodes per day on Yahoo's long-running clusters. On a 4,000-node cluster that is roughly 8 to 12 node failures daily, confirming the GFS assumption that failure is normal and repair must be automatic.

quiz.q: Using Shvachko's numbers, roughly how much NameNode RAM do 500 million average files need?
quiz.a: About 600 bytes x 500 million, roughly 300 GB of RAM.

title: The second NameNode limit: one Java process answering every RPC
body: Besides RAM, the NameNode's second limit is RPC throughput. Every open, list and block report is an RPC to one Java process. Garbage collection (GC) pauses on a huge Java heap make this worse: while the JVM pauses to reclaim memory, requests queue up. Uber reported NameNode RPC queue times of 500 ms at peak in late 2016, versus a normal 10 ms. A NameNode can have plenty of memory and still be too slow because too many clients ask it things at once.
deeper:
The two limits interact. A bigger namespace needs a bigger heap. A bigger heap makes GC pauses longer or more frequent. Longer pauses raise RPC latency for every client, including DataNodes sending block reports, which then add more load.

Block reports are a hidden cost of the GFS-inherited design. Because DataNodes are the source of truth for block locations, thousands of DataNodes periodically send lists of every block they hold, each of which the NameNode must process.

A 50x jump in queue time, from 10 ms to 500 ms, means every job in the cluster slows down, since tasks cannot start until their file opens return. Uber's fixes included tuning GC on its 160 GB NameNode heap, which cut GC pause time from 13% to 1.7%, splitting the namespace, and adopting the Observer NameNode to offload reads. LinkedIn later found that switching the NameNode lock to non-fair mode gave about 10x better performance, another sign that the bottleneck was contention inside one process.

quiz.q: Why do GC pauses make the HDFS NameNode's RPC bottleneck worse as the namespace grows?
quiz.a: A bigger namespace needs a bigger Java heap, which causes longer GC pauses; during pauses every RPC queues, so latency spikes for all clients.

title: HDFS Federation: several NameNodes, each owning part of the tree
body: Federation, added in Hadoop 2, runs multiple independent NameNodes, each owning a separate namespace. Each namespace has its own block pool. DataNodes store blocks for all pools and report to all NameNodes, so storage stays shared. Clients see one tree through ViewFs mount tables or through Router-based Federation. This is static partitioning: operators decide which directory lives on which NameNode, and a hot directory stays hot because it is still served by just one NameNode.
deeper:
Federation multiplies metadata capacity by the number of NameNodes: more RAM, more CPU, more RPC handlers in total. Sharing DataNodes across pools means disks are not stranded per namespace.

ViewFs is a client-side mount table, similar to mounting several file systems into one tree on a Unix machine; paths under one prefix go to one NameNode and paths under another go elsewhere. Router-based Federation moves that mapping into routers so clients do not all need to carry the mount table.

The weaknesses follow from static partitioning. Balancing is manual; someone must notice a NameNode is overloaded and move directories. Moving data between namespaces is a copy, not a metadata rename, because different NameNodes own different trees. And a single very busy directory cannot be split across NameNodes at all.

It is an easy step up from one master, and Uber used it, splitting HDFS into namespaces behind ViewFs. But it postpones rather than solves metadata scaling, unlike the distributed database approach of Colossus and Tectonic.

quiz.q: Why is HDFS Federation called static partitioning, and what is its main weakness?
quiz.a: Operators assign directories to NameNodes by hand; hot directories stay hot on one NameNode, balancing is manual, and cross-namespace moves are copies.

title: HDFS high availability: a quorum of JournalNodes and one writer
body: HDFS high availability with the Quorum Journal Manager (QJM) removes the NameNode single point of failure. The active NameNode writes each edit to a majority of an odd number (at least 3) of JournalNodes. Standby NameNodes tail those edits and must read all of them before becoming active. Only one NameNode may write to the JournalNodes, which prevents split brain, and fencing stops an old active. The ZKFailoverController (ZKFC) uses ZooKeeper for health checks and automatic failover.
deeper:
The majority rule is what makes the journal durable. With 3 JournalNodes, an edit is safe once 2 have it, so one JournalNode can fail without losing edits or blocking writes. With 5, two can fail.

Split brain is the danger of two NameNodes both believing they are active and accepting conflicting writes. QJM prevents it by allowing only one writer to the JournalNodes: a new active takes over writing rights, and the old active's writes are rejected. Fencing additionally ensures the old active cannot keep serving.

Requiring a standby to read all edits before becoming active guarantees it has the full namespace state and does not lose acknowledged changes.

ZKFC runs beside each NameNode, monitors its health, and uses ZooKeeper for leader election. When the active fails, the ZKFC of a healthy standby triggers failover without human action.

Note what HA does not do: it does not add capacity. There is still one active NameNode handling all writes and, until observers, all reads. HA addresses availability, not scaling.

quiz.q: How does the Quorum Journal Manager prevent split brain between two HDFS NameNodes?
quiz.a: Only one NameNode may write to the JournalNodes, and fencing stops an old active, so two actives can never both commit edits.

title: Observer NameNode: serve reads from followers without stale answers
body: The Observer NameNode (design in HDFS-12943) attacks RPC load. Most NameNode traffic is reads, so an Observer tails the edit log and serves reads while the active NameNode serves writes. The hard part is read-your-writes consistency: a client that just created a file must see it. The client tracks the latest transaction ID (state ID) it has seen, and the observer waits until it has caught up to that ID before answering. For consistency across clients, msync() fetches the active's current state ID.
deeper:
Observers build on HA's edit-tailing: like standbys, they follow the JournalNodes, but instead of waiting to take over, they answer read RPCs.

The state-ID protocol works as follows. Each write on the active gets a transaction ID, which is returned to the client. When that client then sends a read to an observer, it includes the highest ID it has seen. If the observer has not yet applied that edit, it holds the request until it catches up, so the client never sees a world older than its own writes.

That covers one client. If client A writes and tells client B out of band, B has not seen A's state ID. B can call msync() to fetch the active's current state ID first, then read from an observer consistently.

The payoff is large: LinkedIn reports observers handle reads that are about 95% of operations, RPC latency dropped to 1 to 2 ms from under 10 ms, and namespace throughput rose about 3x. The limit remains that writes still go to one node.

quiz.q: How does an Observer NameNode avoid returning stale data to a client that just wrote a file?
quiz.a: The client sends the latest state ID it has seen; the observer waits until it has applied edits up to that ID before answering. msync() handles cross-client cases.

title: Hadoop 3 erasure coding: 50% overhead instead of 200%
body: Hadoop 3 added striped erasure coding. Instead of storing whole blocks on one DataNode, a file is split into small cells (1 MB in the built-in policies) striped across a group of DataNodes. The default policy, RS-6-3-1024k, uses 6 data and 3 parity cells, cutting storage overhead from 200% extra with 3x replication to 50% extra: 6 blocks' worth of data takes 9 blocks of space instead of 18. The price is new constraints on hardware layout and supported operations.
deeper:
The constraints are substantial. RS(6,3) needs at least 9 DataNodes and 3 racks (ideally 9 racks) to place a stripe's fragments across failure domains. Most erasure coding traffic crosses racks, both for writes and for rebuilding lost cells, so network bisection bandwidth, the capacity between halves of the network, becomes critical.

Several file operations do not work on EC files: append(), truncate(), concat() and hflush(). Striping and parity make in-place growth and flushing partial stripes difficult, since changing any cell requires updating parity.

Those limits define where EC fits: warm and cold data that is written once and read occasionally. Hot, frequently appended data stays replicated.

This is the same space-versus-flexibility trade seen elsewhere in the chapter. Azure replicates active extents and erasure codes them only after sealing. Tectonic's blob storage replicates first and re-encodes to RS(10,4) later, while its warehouse writes RS(9,6) directly because its files are written whole. HDFS chose striping per file, suited to data that is already complete.

quiz.q: Why does Hadoop 3 erasure coding suit warm and cold data rather than hot data?
quiz.a: append, truncate, concat and hflush don't work on EC files, and most EC traffic crosses racks, so it fits write-once data read occasionally.

title: Yahoo and Uber: HDFS at 4,000 nodes and 400% growth
body: Yahoo in 2010 ran the biggest HDFS clusters of the time: 4,000 nodes and 14 PB, with one namespace holding over 100 million objects. Uber, reporting in 2018, saw HDFS data grow 400% in 2017 alone. Uber's response was a toolkit of fixes: split HDFS into namespaces behind ViewFs, upgrade HDFS, tune garbage collection on a 160 GB NameNode heap, build a 'stitcher' to merge small files, set quotas, and adopt the Observer NameNode.
deeper:
Uber's list is a case study in attacking every NameNode limit at once.

Splitting namespaces behind ViewFs is federation, adding NameNodes so each carries less.

GC tuning on the 160 GB heap cut GC pause time from 13% to 1.7% of the time. Recall Uber had seen RPC queue times of 500 ms at peak in late 2016 versus a normal 10 ms; GC pauses on a huge heap make such RPC queues worse.

The stitcher merges many small files into fewer large ones. Since each file costs roughly the same NameNode memory regardless of size, merging directly frees namespace capacity.

Quotas cap growth at the source.

Observer NameNodes offload read RPCs from the active.

Yahoo's clusters were the basis for Shvachko's analysis. Note the units: Yahoo's figure is 100 million objects (files plus blocks), while his 60 GB estimate is for 100 million files, about 300 million objects. Together, Yahoo and Uber show a decade of HDFS operators hitting the same single-master limits GFS hit, and responding with the same families of fixes.

quiz.q: Why did Uber build a 'stitcher' to merge small files in HDFS?
quiz.a: Each file costs about the same NameNode memory regardless of size, so merging small files frees namespace capacity, the resource that was running out.

title: LinkedIn's exabyte club: 1 billion objects on one NameNode
body: In 'The Exabyte Club' (2021), LinkedIn reported 1 exabyte of total storage across Hadoop clusters. Its largest cluster had 10,000 nodes and 500 PB, with about 1 billion objects on a single NameNode using a 380 GB heap. From 2015 to 2020 it grew from 20 PB to 500 PB, and from 145 million to 1.6 billion namespace objects, with peak load of 250K operations per second. It shows how far a single-writer NameNode can be pushed with enough engineering.
deeper:
LinkedIn's techniques target the NameNode directly.

Observer NameNodes handle reads, which are about 95% of operations. RPC latency dropped to 1 to 2 ms with observers, versus under 10 ms before, and namespace throughput rose about 3x.

A separate Satellite cluster of just 32 DataNodes holds about 100 million small files, away from the main namespace. The data volume is tiny, but the file count is large, so isolating it protects the main NameNode's memory and RPC capacity.

Switching the NameNode lock to non-fair mode gave about 10x better performance. A fair lock hands access strictly in arrival order, adding overhead under heavy contention; non-fair allows threads to grab the lock opportunistically.

The numbers match Shvachko's rule: about 1 billion objects needing a 380 GB heap is consistent with under 200 bytes per object plus overhead. Other big Hadoop users took different paths: Twitter (now X) described a hybrid plan in 2019 to move part of its Hadoop workloads to Google Cloud, and Meta replaced all its HDFS clusters with Tectonic.

quiz.q: Why did LinkedIn put about 100 million small files on a separate 32-DataNode Satellite cluster?
quiz.a: The files cost NameNode memory and RPCs far out of proportion to their bytes; isolating them protected the main namespace, which was the scarce resource.

title: Small files in HDFS are a capacity problem, not a tuning problem
body: Common mistake: treating 'small files' as a performance tuning problem. In HDFS, small files are a capacity problem for the NameNode, because each file costs roughly the same metadata as a large one. A billion 1 KB files cost a billion file objects plus a billion block objects while storing only about 1 TB. LinkedIn and Uber both built special handling, a separate Satellite cluster, a file stitcher, and quotas, because the namespace, not the disks, ran out first.
deeper:
The root is how the NameNode accounts for memory: fewer than 200 bytes per object, whether that object is a file or a block. Disk usage scales with bytes, but NameNode memory scales with object count. With plenty of disk space and a namespace near its limit, the cluster is effectively full.

Treating it as tuning leads to the wrong fixes: adjusting buffer sizes, caching, or job parallelism does nothing for a heap that is filling with file objects. The right fixes change the object count or where objects live: merge files (Uber's stitcher), cap creation (quotas), or isolate small-file workloads in their own namespace (LinkedIn's Satellite cluster).

The same logic applied to GFS: its limits list starts with file count, not bytes. And it is the core reason newer systems moved metadata into distributed databases or packed small objects into big units. Azure's stream layer tracks 1 GB extents, not objects, and keeps object indexing in a separate scalable layer, avoiding the problem structurally rather than managing it operationally.

quiz.q: Why are small files a capacity problem, not just a performance problem, in HDFS?
quiz.a: Each file costs about the same NameNode memory regardless of size, so many small files exhaust the namespace before the disks fill.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
title: Before Tectonic: IOPS stranded in one system, space in another
body: Before Tectonic, Meta ran separate systems: Haystack for hot blobs (3x replication plus RAID-6, ideally 3.6x), f4 for warm blobs (RS(10,4) in two datacenters, about 2.8x), and many HDFS clusters for the data warehouse. Each system stranded resources. Haystack was IOPS-bound and its effective replication rose to 5.3x, while f4 had spare IOPS but ran out of capacity. The fix: one multi-tenant file system big enough to put blob storage and the warehouse on the same disks.
deeper:
Stranding means a resource sits idle in one system while another system is starved of it. Haystack needed many disks for their IOPS, not their capacity, so it bought far more space than it filled, pushing the effective replication factor from an ideal 3.6x to 5.3x. f4 had the opposite problem: idle disk arms but full disks.

Workload drift made it worse. More blobs were short-lived and were deleted before ever migrating from Haystack to f4, so more data lived its whole life at Haystack's expensive storage factor.

The warehouse ran on many separate HDFS clusters, each a single-NameNode system with its own metadata ceiling.

The insight behind Tectonic is complementary demand. Blob storage is IOPS-heavy relative to its bytes; the warehouse is capacity-heavy with bursts of throughput. On shared disks, one tenant's spare IOPS cover the other's needs, and vice versa. That requires a single file system large enough, exabytes in one datacenter, and flexible enough to serve both, which in turn requires metadata that scales far beyond an HDFS NameNode.

quiz.q: Why did Haystack's effective replication factor rise to 5.3x when its ideal was 3.6x?
quiz.a: Haystack was IOPS-bound, so it needed more disks for their operations than for their space, leaving capacity idle; short-lived blobs also never moved to cheaper f4.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
title: Tectonic: a datacenter-wide file system on plain XFS disks
body: A Tectonic cluster can span an entire datacenter and store exabytes. It has three big parts: a Chunk Store for data, a Metadata Store, and a Client Library, plus background services. In the Chunk Store, storage nodes keep chunks as files on local XFS, plus a 1 TB SSD per node for XFS metadata and hot chunks. To upper layers a block looks like an array of bytes, but it is really a set of replicated or Reed-Solomon encoded chunks spread across storage nodes.
deeper:
The layering separates what callers see from how data is protected. A file is a list of blocks; a block is an abstract byte range; the chunks underneath provide redundancy. Whether a block is three replicas or an RS stripe is a per-block decision made by the client, invisible to anyone reading it as bytes.

The 1 TB SSD is a small but important detail. HDDs are slow at the small random reads that file system metadata requires, so putting XFS metadata on SSD keeps local lookups fast, and hot chunks benefit too.

Storing chunks on XFS contrasts with Ceph, which abandoned local file systems for BlueStore on raw devices. The difference is workload: Tectonic mostly writes large immutable chunks, which local file systems handle well, while Ceph needed fine-grained updates and transactions that file systems handled poorly.

The cluster-per-datacenter scale is what makes consolidation work: a single pool large enough for blob storage and the warehouse together, so their complementary demands can balance out on the same disks.

quiz.q: Why can Tectonic keep chunks on XFS when Ceph found local file systems a poor backend?
quiz.a: Tectonic mostly writes large immutable chunks, which file systems handle well; Ceph needed fine-grained updates and transactions, which they handled poorly.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
title: Tectonic splits metadata into Name, File and Block layers
body: Tectonic's Metadata Store is the heart of its scaling. Metadata is disaggregated into three layers: a Name layer mapping each directory to its children, a File layer mapping each file to its blocks, and a Block layer mapping each block to disk locations, plus a reverse index for repair. Each layer lives in ZippyDB, Meta's linearizable, sharded key-value store running RocksDB on SSD, and each layer is hash-partitioned so load spreads evenly across shards.
deeper:
Splitting by kind lets each layer scale and cache independently. Namespace operations like listing a directory hit the Name layer. Opening and reading a file hits the File and Block layers. Repair hits the Block layer's reverse index, which answers 'which blocks lived on this failed disk?' without scanning everything.

Each layer has a different access pattern. Name entries change when files are created or renamed. File-to-block mappings are mostly written once. Block locations change with repair and rebalancing. Separate layers let each be scaled and cached for its own pattern.

ZippyDB's linearizability gives strong consistency for metadata: operations appear to happen in a single order, matching Tectonic's model of a single writer per file with linearizable metadata.

The cost is more moving parts and more RPC hops: opening a file may touch several layers. The chapter's summary table lists 'layered metadata by kind' as its own approach, shared with Azure's split between the stream layer and partition layer and with ADLS, which layers metadata but partitions it differently.

quiz.q: What does Tectonic's Block layer reverse index make easy?
quiz.a: Repair: finding which blocks were stored on a failed disk without scanning all metadata.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
title: Hash vs range partitioning: why Tectonic chose to scatter metadata
body: Tectonic hash-partitions each metadata layer. The paper contrasts this with Azure Data Lake Store (ADLS), which also layers metadata but range-partitions it. Range partitioning keeps related entries together, such as all entries of one directory, which is good for scans like listing a directory. But a busy directory then becomes a hot spot, because all its traffic lands on one shard. Hashing spreads load evenly across shards, at the cost of harder multi-item operations.
deeper:
In range partitioning, keys are sorted and each shard owns a contiguous range. Entries sharing a prefix, like the children of one directory, land on the same shard. A directory listing is one efficient scan. But if thousands of jobs create files in the same directory, that one shard takes all the load, and adding shards does not help unless the range can be split.

In hash partitioning, each key is hashed to a shard, so neighboring keys scatter. Load from a busy directory spreads across many shards instead of pinning one. The downside: operations touching multiple items, such as a recursive listing or rename spanning many entries, now span many shards and need more coordination.

Tectonic's choice reflects its workloads: many tenants with busy directories and very high metadata rates, where even load matters more than scan efficiency. This is a general database design trade, not unique to file systems, and the same question applies to any sharded metadata: do your hottest operations need locality, or does even load matter more?

quiz.q: Why did Tectonic choose hash partitioning for its metadata layers instead of range partitioning?
quiz.a: Range partitioning puts related entries, like a busy directory, on one shard and creates hot spots; hashing spreads load evenly, at the cost of harder multi-item operations.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
title: Tectonic's clients do the work; background services clean up
body: Tectonic is a client-driven microservice architecture. The Client Library orchestrates calls to the metadata and storage services and does replication or Reed-Solomon encoding itself, so each tenant can tune behavior to its workload. Background services run garbage collection, repair, rebalancing and rack drains. They also manage copysets, which are the distinct combinations of disks holding a block, to balance the risk of data loss against the load of reconstruction.
deeper:
Client-driven means there is no central proxy that all data passes through. The client talks to the Metadata Store to find or allocate blocks, then writes chunks directly to storage nodes, deciding encoding and placement parameters on the way. This is the same shape as the Colossus client library with its software RAID.

Copysets deserve explanation. If blocks are scattered across random disk combinations, nearly any simultaneous failure of a few disks will destroy some block, though only a little data. If blocks use only a few fixed combinations, losses are rarer but larger, and rebuilding a failed disk draws from fewer peers, making reconstruction slower. Managing copysets lets Tectonic choose a point between those extremes.

Rack drains move data off a rack before maintenance or decommissioning, another routine background task at datacenter scale.

Keeping repair and rebalancing in background services, not in clients or metadata servers keeps that work off the foreground path, mirroring Colossus custodians.

quiz.q: What trade-off do Tectonic's copysets manage?
quiz.a: The number of distinct disk combinations holding blocks: fewer combinations make data loss rarer but rebuilds slower; more spread rebuild load but raise loss likelihood.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
title: Warehouse tenant: buffer a full block, RS-encode, write directly
body: The most important idea in Tectonic is tenant-specific optimization: one file system, but each tenant writes differently. The data warehouse writes large files once and reads them after they are complete. So its client buffers a full block, RS-encodes it in memory, and writes the chunks directly. Long-lived data typically uses RS(9,6), 9 data plus 6 parity chunks across 15 disks. Short-lived data like MapReduce shuffle files uses RS(3,3). This saves space, disk I/O and network compared with replication.
deeper:
Encoding in memory is possible because nobody reads a warehouse file until it is finished. The client can wait to accumulate a whole block, compute parity once, and write each chunk exactly once. No replicated intermediate copy is ever written, so there is no later re-encoding cost.

The two codes fit different lifetimes. RS(9,6) stores 15 chunks for 9 of data, about 1.67x, and tolerates up to 6 lost chunks, strong durability for data that lives a long time. RS(3,3) is 2x overhead but only 6 chunks, simpler to write and fast to read, suited to shuffle files that exist only for the duration of a job. Even at 2x, it is cheaper than 3x replication.

This is only possible because encoding lives in the client library. A system that encoded on the server side with a single global policy could not give the warehouse bulk-encoded writes while simultaneously giving blob storage low-latency replicated appends. Per-tenant clients are the escape hatch that makes consolidation practical.

quiz.q: Why can Tectonic's data warehouse RS-encode data in memory before writing it?
quiz.a: Warehouse files are large, written once, and read only when complete, so the client can buffer a full block, encode it, and write each chunk once.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
title: Blob tenant: replicate now, encode later, and hedge the writes
body: Tectonic's blob storage needs low latency for small writes. It uses a replicated quorum append: write to replicas and acknowledge once a quorum has the data. After the block is sealed, the client re-encodes it to RS(10,4) with one large I/O on each of 14 nodes. This is the same 'replicate now, encode later' pattern Azure uses. The client can also hedge writes, sending to more nodes than needed and taking the fastest acknowledgments, to cut tail latency.
deeper:
Why not encode each blob append directly? RS-encoding each small append would require writes to all 14 nodes of an RS(10,4) stripe, costing many I/Os for a few kilobytes. Replicating the append to a quorum of replicas is far cheaper and faster. Once the block is full and sealed, the client encodes it once, turning many small writes into 14 large sequential ones and dropping the storage cost.

Quorum acknowledgment means a slow replica does not delay the write; hedging goes further by deliberately over-sending so the fastest responders win. Both target tail latency, the slowest few percent of requests, which dominates user-facing experience.

Isolation is handled coarsely: performance is managed across tens of traffic groups with similar latency needs, not hundreds of individual applications. Grouping keeps the isolation mechanism manageable while still preventing a bulk warehouse job from starving latency-sensitive blob traffic.
