Together with the warehouse path, this shows one storage layer serving two opposite write patterns by letting each tenant's client choose its own write protocol.

quiz.q: Why does Tectonic's blob storage replicate first and re-encode to RS(10,4) later?
quiz.a: Blob writes are small and latency-sensitive; RS-encoding each append costs many I/Os (14 for RS(10,4)), so blobs replicate for fast quorum acks and encode once after sealing.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
title: Tectonic results: 1,590 PB, 10.7B files, 10x fewer clusters
body: One representative multi-tenant Tectonic production cluster had 1,590 PB of capacity, 1,250 PB used (about 70%), 10.7 billion files, 15 billion blocks and 4,208 storage nodes. Blob storage used about 49% of the space and the warehouse about 51%. Tectonic served around ten tenants and fully replaced Haystack, f4 and HDFS. Warehouse clusters fell 10x in number. Blob storage reached an effective replication factor of about 2.8x, versus Haystack's 5.3x.
deeper:
The numbers validate both halves of the design. On metadata: 10.7 billion files and 15 billion blocks in a single cluster would be far beyond any HDFS NameNode; LinkedIn's largest held about 1 billion objects. The hash-partitioned ZippyDB layers made that possible.

On economics: blob storage's effective factor falling from 5.3x to about 2.8x means roughly half the raw disk for the same data. Replicate-then-encode with RS(10,4) keeps blob data cheap, and on shared disks blob storage no longer strands capacity to get IOPS.

The sharing ran both ways: the warehouse absorbed traffic spikes using blob storage's spare IOPS. That is the complementary-demand argument working in production.

The near 50/50 split of space between blob storage and the warehouse matters too: both tenants are large enough that their spare resources meaningfully cover each other.

Cutting warehouse clusters by 10x also reduces operational load: fewer clusters to upgrade, monitor and balance, and less capacity stranded in per-cluster headroom.

quiz.q: How did consolidating onto Tectonic help the data warehouse, not just blob storage?
quiz.a: The warehouse absorbed traffic spikes using blob storage's spare IOPS on the shared disks, and its clusters fell 10x in number.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
title: Meta's GenAI clusters checkpoint through a flash-optimized Tectonic
body: In 2024, Meta said its 24,576-GPU GenAI training clusters use a FUSE API backed by a version of Tectonic optimized for flash. FUSE lets a user-space file system appear as a normal mounted directory, so training code can use ordinary file operations. This lets thousands of GPUs save and load checkpoints together. Meta also deployed Hammerspace, a parallel NFS system, for interactive developer use, pairing a scalable storage backend with a friendlier interface for humans.
deeper:
Checkpoints are the critical storage workload in large-model training. Periodically, every GPU writes its part of the model state at the same moment, and after a failure, all of them read it back together. While storage absorbs the checkpoint, GPUs sit idle, so checkpoint speed directly determines how much expensive compute is wasted.

A flash-optimized Tectonic handles the burst: SSDs sustain the parallel write and read bandwidth that HDD-based clusters cannot. Exposing it through FUSE means frameworks can checkpoint with standard file APIs rather than a custom client.

Hammerspace serves a different need: developers exploring data interactively want familiar NFS semantics and responsiveness.

Meta says optimizing checkpoints cut synchronization to hundreds of milliseconds across thousands of ranks (a rank is one training process).

This connects Tectonic to the chapter's later point that AI training brought parallel file systems back. Training looks like HPC, thousands of clients reading and writing in lockstep, and demands storage built for synchronized bandwidth, not just capacity.

quiz.q: Why does checkpoint storage speed matter so much for large GPU training clusters?
quiz.a: Thousands of GPUs checkpoint at the same moment and sit idle until storage absorbs it, so slow checkpoints directly waste expensive compute.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
title: Consolidation wins only with isolation and escape hatches
body: Senior staff lens: Tectonic's lesson is economic. Specialized systems strand IOPS in one place and capacity in another. A shared multi-tenant layer can reclaim that waste, but it wins only if it also provides isolation, such as Tectonic's traffic groups, and tenant-specific escape hatches, such as client-side encoding. Without them, consolidation creates noisy-neighbor outages, where one tenant's burst degrades everyone else sharing the disks.
deeper:
The argument for consolidation is pooling: combining workloads with different peaks and different resource profiles reduces total hardware, as Meta's blob storage factor falling from 5.3x to about 2.8x showed.

But pooling has two failure modes. Without isolation, a large warehouse scan can saturate disks and push blob storage latency past what users tolerate. Traffic groups, tens of them grouping applications with similar latency needs, give the system a manageable way to prioritize and limit.

Without escape hatches, a one-size-fits-all design forces every tenant into a compromise. If Tectonic had only one write path, either the warehouse would pay replication costs or blob storage would pay encoding latency. Client-side encoding lets each tenant keep what made its specialized system good.

When evaluating a proposal to merge storage systems, look for both. Savings on paper come from pooling; whether they survive production depends on isolation and per-tenant flexibility. Missing either one tends to show up later as incidents and exceptions that erode the savings.

quiz.q: What two features must a consolidated multi-tenant storage layer provide to avoid noisy-neighbor problems?
quiz.a: Performance isolation (like Tectonic's traffic groups) and tenant-specific escape hatches (like client-side encoding choices).

section: Microsoft Azure Storage: the stream layer (SOSP 2011)
title: Azure storage is built from stamps of 10 to 20 racks
body: Windows Azure Storage (WAS) is the storage behind Azure Blobs, Tables and Queues. Its 2011 SOSP paper describes a design with strong consistency from the start. WAS is built from storage stamps: a stamp is a cluster of 10 to 20 racks with 18 disk-heavy storage nodes per rack. First-generation stamps held about 2 PB raw, next-generation stamps up to 30 PB. In 2011, WAS had 70 PB of raw storage in production.
deeper:
A stamp is the unit of deployment and scale. Rather than one giant cluster, Azure grows by adding stamps, each a self-contained storage system with its own layers.

A Location Service sits above the stamps. It assigns customer accounts to stamps and migrates accounts when a stamp reaches about 70% utilization. This keeps stamps from running full and gives headroom for failures, growth and rebalancing.

The stamp model bounds the problem each metadata service must solve: no stamp exceeds a known size, so internal metadata can be sized for that ceiling. Scaling beyond one stamp happens at the account-routing level, not inside a single metadata service.

Strong consistency from the start is a notable contrast with GFS's relaxed model. A plausible reason (an inference, not stated in the paper summary) is that Azure served external customers, who could not be asked to handle duplicates and garbage regions the way GFS's internal teams did.

quiz.q: What does the Azure Location Service do when a stamp reaches about 70% utilization?
quiz.a: It migrates accounts to other stamps, keeping headroom in each stamp for failures, growth and rebalancing.

section: Microsoft Azure Storage: the stream layer (SOSP 2011)
title: Inside a stamp: front-end, partition and stream layers
body: Each Azure storage stamp has three layers. The front-end layer is stateless servers that authenticate requests and route them. The partition layer understands Blobs, Tables and Queues; it range-partitions objects across partition servers and does inter-stamp (geo) replication asynchronously. The stream layer is the distributed file system: it stores bits on disk and does intra-stamp replication synchronously. Each layer has one job, and the stream layer never needs to know what a blob or table is.
deeper:
The split of replication is deliberate. Inside a stamp, the stream layer replicates synchronously: a write is acknowledged only after replicas have it, giving strong consistency and durability against disk and node failures. Between stamps, in different regions, the partition layer replicates asynchronously, because waiting for a distant datacenter on every write would add large latency. Geo-replication protects against disasters while keeping the write path fast.

The partition layer does the object-level work: it knows that a blob named X lives at a given offset in a given stream, and it splits the key space into ranges assigned to partition servers. Range partitioning keeps related objects together, useful for listing and for table scans.

The stream layer is kept deliberately dumb. It deals only in streams and extents, large append-only units, which is what keeps its metadata small.

This layered design splits metadata by kind: object-level metadata in the partition layer, storage-level metadata in the stream layer. Each can be scaled and optimized independently, a theme the chapter's metadata table highlights as a distinct approach.

quiz.q: Why does Azure replicate synchronously within a stamp but asynchronously between stamps?
quiz.a: Synchronous intra-stamp replication gives strong consistency against local failures; waiting on distant stamps for every write would add too much latency, so geo-replication is async.

section: Microsoft Azure Storage: the stream layer (SOSP 2011)
title: Streams and extents: big append-only units with sealed history
body: In the Azure stream layer, a stream is an ordered list of pointers to extents and looks like one big append-only file. An extent is a sequence of appended blocks with a target size of 1 GB, and many small objects are packed into one extent. Only the last extent of a stream can be appended to; earlier extents are sealed and immutable. A Paxos-replicated Stream Manager tracks streams and extents, and Extent Nodes store the replicas.
deeper:
Sealing is central. Once an extent reaches its size target or is otherwise closed, it never changes again. Immutable data is easy to replicate, cache, move and erasure code, since no concurrent writer can invalidate a copy.

Packing many small objects into a 1 GB extent solves the small-files problem structurally. The storage layer sees a modest number of large extents, not billions of tiny objects.

Because a stream is just a list of extent pointers, appending to a stream means appending to its last extent.

Paxos replication makes the Stream Manager fault tolerant: its state is agreed among several replicas, so losing one does not lose metadata or availability.

This design shares DNA with GFS (append-heavy, large units, a central manager) but avoids GFS's weak points: consistency is strong, the manager is replicated, and the manager tracks far fewer, larger units. Colossus and Tectonic later converged on similar append-only, seal-then-encode storage.

quiz.q: Why does sealing extents make them easier to manage?
quiz.a: Sealed extents are immutable, so they can be replicated, moved, cached and erasure coded without worrying about concurrent writers invalidating copies.

section: Microsoft Azure Storage: the stream layer (SOSP 2011)
title: Why a 30 PB Azure stamp's metadata fits in memory
body: The Azure Stream Manager tracks only extents, not objects. A 30 PB stamp with 1 GB extents has about 30 million extents before replication, which fits comfortably in memory. The object index, which blob sits at which offset of which extent, lives in the range-partitioned partition layer, which scales separately across many partition servers. So Azure splits metadata by kind, not only by key: a small, fast service for big units and a separate scalable layer for small objects.
deeper:
The arithmetic: 30 PB divided by 1 GB is about 30 million extents. Even at a few hundred bytes per extent plus replica locations, that is a few gigabytes to tens of gigabytes, manageable for one Paxos-replicated service.

Compare HDFS: a NameNode tracks every file and every block, so billions of small files mean billions of objects in one heap. Azure's stream layer never sees individual objects at all. The fine-grained metadata still exists, but it lives in the partition layer, which can split and rebalance ranges across servers as load changes.

The chapter calls this 'big units, small index elsewhere'. Its strength is tiny metadata at the bottom layer. Its weakness is needing a second scalable index layer to find objects.

This is a powerful design move: instead of making one metadata service scale to everything, make the lower layer's units so big that its metadata stays small, and push per-object detail to a layer designed for it. Tectonic's blocks and Colossus's layers show the same instinct.

quiz.q: Why can the Azure Stream Manager keep its metadata in memory even for a 30 PB stamp?
quiz.a: It tracks only 1 GB extents, about 30 million for 30 PB; the per-object index lives in the separately scaled partition layer.

section: Microsoft Azure Storage: the stream layer (SOSP 2011)
title: Azure erasure codes extents once they seal: 3x down to about 1.3x
body: Active Azure extents are replicated 3 times, which makes appends fast and simple. When an extent is sealed, WAS erasure codes it in the background and then deletes the full replicas, bringing storage cost down from 3x to about 1.3x to 1.5x. The 2012 follow-up paper introduced LRC(12,2,2), a Local Reconstruction Code with 1.33x overhead, where rebuilding a single lost fragment reads 6 fragments instead of 12, laid out across 20 fault domains and 10 upgrade domains.
deeper:
The seal-then-encode pattern gets the best of both: replication for the mutable tail, where writes must be fast and small, and erasure coding for the immutable bulk, where space efficiency matters most. Since only the last extent of each stream is active, nearly all data ends up encoded.

LRC improves on plain Reed-Solomon for the common case. In LRC(12,2,2), 12 data fragments are split into two local groups of 6, each with its own local parity, plus 2 global parities. Most failures lose a single fragment, which can be rebuilt from its local group, reading 6 fragments instead of the 12 a standard RS(12,4) would need. That halves repair traffic and speeds rebuilds, while overhead stays at 16 of 12, about 1.33x.

Fault domains are units that can fail together, such as racks; upgrade domains are groups taken down together during software rollouts. Spreading 16 fragments across 20 fault domains and 10 upgrade domains keeps data readable during both hardware failures and planned upgrades.

quiz.q: What advantage does Azure's LRC(12,2,2) have over plain Reed-Solomon for single-fragment failures?
quiz.a: A single lost fragment is rebuilt from its local group, reading 6 fragments instead of 12, halving repair traffic at about 1.33x overhead.

section: Microsoft Azure Storage: the stream layer (SOSP 2011)
title: Three ideas Azure, Tectonic and Colossus all share
body: In industry: the Azure design, Tectonic's blob path and Colossus share three ideas. First, append-only storage: data is written by appending, never overwritten in place. Second, seal-then-encode: keep the active tail replicated for fast writes, then erasure code it once it is sealed and immutable. Third, a small, fast metadata service tracking big units, extents or blocks, while a separate layer indexes small objects. When you see a new storage design, look for these three.
deeper:
Each idea removes a class of problems.

Append-only eliminates overwrite conflicts and makes replicas easy to compare: a replica is either a prefix of the correct content or it is wrong. It also enables immutability once a unit is closed.

Seal-then-encode resolves the tension between write latency and storage cost. Azure goes from 3x to about 1.3x to 1.5x; Tectonic's blob storage goes from replicated quorum appends to RS(10,4), reaching about 2.8x effective versus Haystack's 5.3x.

Big units with a separate small-object index keep the bottom-layer metadata tiny. Azure's Stream Manager tracks about 30 million extents for a 30 PB stamp; the partition layer indexes objects.

Using these as a checklist is a fast way to understand an unfamiliar system. If a design supports random overwrites, ask how it keeps replicas consistent. If it erasure codes at write time, ask what small writes cost. If one service tracks every object, ask what happens at a billion objects. Missing ideas usually point to where the system will struggle.

quiz.q: What are the three ideas shared by Azure's stream layer, Tectonic's blob path and Colossus?
quiz.a: Append-only storage, seal-then-encode (replicate the active tail, erasure code after sealing), and a small metadata service tracking big units with objects indexed elsewhere.

title: Ceph: one open-source cluster for block, object and file
body: Ceph began as a PhD project by Sage Weil at UC Santa Cruz and became the leading open-source unified storage system. It offers three interfaces on one cluster: block storage (RBD), object storage (RGW, S3-compatible) and a file system (CephFS). All three sit on a common core called RADOS. Ceph's distinctive idea is that it computes where data lives with a formula instead of storing a location table, removing a large part of the metadata problem other systems struggle with.
deeper:
Being unified matters operationally: one cluster and one set of disks can serve virtual machine disks, S3-style applications and shared file systems, instead of running separate systems for each.

RBD exposes block devices, used for virtual machine volumes; DigitalOcean's Block Storage product is built on Ceph. RGW is a gateway speaking an S3-compatible protocol for object storage. CephFS adds a POSIX-like file system with its own metadata servers.

The underlying RADOS layer handles everything below those interfaces: storing objects, replicating or erasure coding them, detecting failures and recovering.

In the chapter's framing, where GFS put metadata in one machine's RAM and Colossus and Tectonic moved it into a database, Ceph attacks the problem differently by eliminating block-location metadata entirely through computed placement. The file system namespace still needs metadata servers, but the mapping from data to disks, the part that grows fastest with data volume, never has to be stored or looked up.

quiz.q: What three storage interfaces does Ceph offer on one cluster?
quiz.a: Block storage (RBD), S3-compatible object storage (RGW) and a file system (CephFS), all on the RADOS core.

title: RADOS: OSDs store objects, monitors hold the cluster map
body: Ceph's core is RADOS, the Reliable Autonomic Distributed Object Store. OSDs (object storage daemons, one per disk) store objects, replicate them to peers and recover data. A small cluster of monitors holds the cluster map: which OSDs exist, which are up, and the placement rules. Objects live in pools, each with its own replication or erasure-coding setting, and each object hashes to a placement group (PG) that maps to a set of OSDs.
deeper:
The division of labor differs from GFS. Monitors do not track where each object lives. They hold only the cluster map, which is small and changes only when hardware or rules change. OSDs are active participants: they replicate to their peers and run recovery themselves, rather than waiting for a master's instructions.

Placement groups are an intermediate level of indirection. Instead of placing millions of objects individually, Ceph hashes each object into one of a manageable number of PGs, and places whole PGs on OSDs. Recovery and rebalancing operate on PGs, which is much cheaper to reason about than per-object tracking.

Pools let different data use different protection settings on the same cluster: a pool of hot virtual machine disks might use replication, while a pool of archival objects uses erasure coding.

The word 'autonomic' reflects the goal of self-management: OSDs detect peer failures, report them, and heal the cluster with minimal central involvement, extending the GFS idea of automatic repair into a more decentralized form.

quiz.q: What does a Ceph placement group (PG) do?
quiz.a: It groups objects: each object hashes to a PG, and whole PGs map to sets of OSDs, so placement and recovery work on PGs instead of individual objects.

title: CRUSH: any client can compute where an object lives
body: Ceph's key invention is CRUSH, a deterministic pseudo-random placement function. Given an object's name and the cluster map, any client can compute which OSDs hold the object. The path is: object name, then hash to a placement group, then CRUSH maps the PG to an ordered list of OSDs. There is no central table of block locations. Clients never ask a metadata server where data is; they calculate it and go straight to the right disks.
deeper:
Deterministic means everyone with the same cluster map gets the same answer. Pseudo-random means placement spreads data evenly across OSDs, as if randomly, without storing the random choices.

The consequences are large. There is no location lookup on the data path, so no metadata server to overload. The location metadata that GFS, HDFS and Tectonic must store, a block-to-disk table, simply does not exist. The only shared state is the cluster map held by monitors, which is small and changes rarely.

Compare this with the other approaches. GFS keeps locations in master RAM, learned from chunkservers. Tectonic keeps them in a Block layer on ZippyDB. Both can move any block anywhere, but must store and scale that mapping. CRUSH gives up some freedom in exchange for no mapping at all. The chapter calls this 'compute placement instead of storing it'.

quiz.q: What metadata does Ceph not need to store because of CRUSH?
quiz.a: A block-to-disk location table: any client computes object placement from the object name and the cluster map.

title: CRUSH turns failure domains into a function, but data must move
body: CRUSH knows the physical hierarchy of the cluster: OSDs, hosts, racks, rows and datacenters. A placement rule can say '3 replicas in 3 different racks' or 'SSD OSDs only'. It is failure-domain thinking turned into a function, and it avoids a single point of failure, a bottleneck, and a physical limit to scale. The trade-off: when the map changes, some data must move, and you cannot place one hot object on a chosen node without changing rules.
deeper:
Rules make durability policy explicit and automatic. Rather than a placement service choosing nodes and hoping it respects failure domains, the function guarantees that replicas land in separate racks or on the right device class, every time, for every client.

The cost appears when the map changes. Adding a disk or losing one changes the inputs to CRUSH, so the computed locations for some placement groups change, and their data must physically migrate. Movement is unavoidable, since location is a function of the map.

The second cost is control. In Tectonic or Colossus, a hot block can be moved or extra-replicated because a table records its location. In Ceph, an object's location is whatever the formula says; changing it for one object means changing rules that affect many.

So the chapter's summary table lists computed placement's strength as 'no block-location table at all' and its weaknesses as 'data moves when the map changes, less control per object'.

quiz.q: What is the main cost of Ceph computing placement with CRUSH instead of storing it?
quiz.a: Data must move when the cluster map changes, and you can't freely place an individual hot object without changing rules that affect many objects.

title: BlueStore: why Ceph gave up on local file systems
body: For a decade, Ceph stored objects as files on local file systems, a design called FileStore. A SOSP 2019 paper explains why it gave up: efficient transactions on a file system were very hard, local metadata performance hurt distributed performance, and support for new hardware was slow to arrive. BlueStore runs directly on raw devices. It became the default in 2017 and was used by 70% of surveyed users in 2018.
deeper:
BlueStore also added capabilities FileStore struggled with: full checksums on all data, inline compression, and fast overwrites of erasure-coded data. Owning the whole storage stack let Ceph implement exactly the semantics it needed rather than emulating them on top of POSIX.

The transaction problem is the heart of it. Ceph operations often need to update data and metadata atomically. The SOSP 2019 paper found that making such transactions efficient on top of a file system was very hard.

The contrast with Tectonic is instructive: Tectonic keeps chunks on XFS and is happy there. The difference is workload. Ceph needs fine-grained updates and transactions, because it serves block devices and file systems with in-place modifications. Tectonic mostly writes large immutable chunks, which local file systems handle well.

The chapter's takeaway phrasing: BlueStore showed that building on local file systems can cost more than it saves. The right answer depends on whether your write pattern matches what the file system is good at.

quiz.q: Why did Ceph move from FileStore to BlueStore on raw devices?
quiz.a: Efficient transactions on a local file system were very hard, local metadata performance hurt distributed performance, and new hardware support lagged.

title: CephFS splits the directory tree across metadata servers
body: CephFS, Ceph's file system, adds metadata servers (MDS) to manage the namespace. Multiple active MDS daemons split the directory tree into subtrees, each owned by one MDS rank. Admins can pin subtrees to specific MDS ranks, or use ephemeral pinning, which hashes directories across ranks. A dynamic balancer can split and move subtrees to less loaded ranks. So even Ceph, which computes data placement, still needs stored metadata for the file namespace.
deeper:
CRUSH solves where object data lives, but a file system also needs names, directories, permissions and file-to-object mappings. That namespace metadata is what the MDS cluster manages.

Subtree partitioning keeps locality: all files in a directory are managed by one MDS, so operations like listing or creating within a directory are handled by one server. The downside mirrors range partitioning: a hot subtree can overload its MDS.

The three balancing options trade control for automation. Static pinning gives predictability but needs human attention. Ephemeral pinning hashes directories across ranks for even load, similar to Tectonic's hash partitioning. The dynamic balancer moves subtrees automatically based on load, but balancing is hard, and moving subtrees has its own cost.

The chapter groups this with Lustre DNE as 'subtree partitioning': strengths are locality for directory operations; weaknesses are hard balancing and hot subtrees. It shows that no single technique removes all metadata: Ceph removed block-location metadata, but namespace metadata still needed its own scaling strategy.

quiz.q: Why does CephFS need metadata servers even though CRUSH computes data placement?
quiz.a: CRUSH only locates object data; the file namespace (directories, names, file-to-object mapping) still needs stored metadata, managed by MDS daemons.

title: Ceph in production: DigitalOcean block storage and a decade at CERN
body: Ceph runs at serious scale in production. DigitalOcean built its Block Storage product in 2016 on Ceph, all-SSD with 3 replicas across separate servers and racks. CERN, the European physics laboratory, has run Ceph for about a decade and presented a '10 years retrospective' in 2023. Both show Ceph's appeal: an open-source system that can provide multi-petabyte, self-healing storage without relying on a single vendor or a hyperscaler's in-house software.
deeper:
DigitalOcean's choice illustrates Ceph's block interface. RBD provides virtual disks for cloud servers; placing 3 replicas across separate servers and racks is exactly the kind of rule CRUSH expresses directly. All-SSD fits the latency needs of virtual machine disks, which see many small random reads and writes.

CERN's decade of use shows longevity. Running one storage system across ten years means living through hardware generations and data growth. Ceph's computed placement helps here: adding new hardware changes the cluster map, and data rebalances automatically, though that rebalancing is also the data movement cost CRUSH trades for having no location table.

These users differ from Google or Meta: they run storage built by others rather than building their own. For such organizations, Ceph's combination of open source, unified interfaces and no single metadata server for data placement is its main attraction.

quiz.q: Why is Ceph a good fit for DigitalOcean's block storage with replicas across servers and racks?
quiz.a: RBD provides virtual disks, and CRUSH rules directly express placement like 3 replicas on separate servers and racks; all-SSD fits VM disk latency needs.

section: Lustre and GPFS: HPC and AI training
title: Lustre: stripe one huge file across many servers for bandwidth
body: High-performance computing (HPC) differs from web workloads: thousands of compute nodes read and write the same huge files in parallel, with strict POSIX semantics, over very fast networks like InfiniBand. Lustre serves this with a management server (MGS), metadata servers and targets (MDS/MDT) holding the namespace and file layouts, and object storage servers and targets (OSS/OST) holding data. Kernel clients get a layout from the MDT, then read and write many OSTs directly.
deeper:
Striping is the key feature. One file is spread across many OSTs, so a single file gets the bandwidth of many servers. When thousands of processes each read their own part of a huge simulation file, their requests hit different OSTs simultaneously.

Clients run in the kernel, presenting a regular POSIX file system to applications. Strict POSIX semantics matter to HPC codes written against standard file APIs, unlike GFS or HDFS, which use custom, non-POSIX interfaces.

The layout is Lustre's version of the GFS pattern: fetch where data lives from the metadata service once, then go directly to storage servers.

DNE (Distributed Namespace) lets multiple MDTs split the namespace, adding metadata capacity. Even so, the Tectonic paper notes Lustre's weak point: it limits the number of metadata nodes, which limits scalability.

At Oak Ridge, the Frontier supercomputer uses Orion, a Lustre file system on HPE ClusterStor with 679 PB of usable namespace and separate performance and capacity OST pools, pairing fast storage for active work with cheaper bulk storage.

quiz.q: How does Lustre give a single file the bandwidth of many servers?
quiz.a: Striping: the file is spread across many OSTs, and clients, after getting the layout from the MDT, read and write those OSTs directly in parallel.

section: Lustre and GPFS: HPC and AI training
title: HPC file systems are built for giant files, not billions of small ones
body: The Tectonic paper notes the weak point of HPC file systems: Lustre and GPFS are tuned for high-throughput parallel access, but Lustre limits the number of metadata nodes, which limits scalability. HPC file systems are built for bandwidth to a few enormous files, not for billions of small files. GPFS, IBM's parallel file system (now IBM Spectrum Scale / Storage Scale), is widely used in HPC and enterprise; Oak Ridge's previous flagship, Summit, used a 250 PB GPFS file system with 2.5 TB/s of bandwidth.
deeper:
The contrast with web-scale systems is about what is scarce. A supercomputer simulation might have thousands of processes writing to one checkpoint file or a handful of huge output files. Metadata operations are few; bandwidth is everything. Striping and fast networks deliver it.

A web company's data warehouse or blob store is the opposite: billions of files, many small, with metadata operations at hundreds of thousands per second. A design with a limited number of metadata nodes struggles here, which is the limitation the Tectonic paper points out.

GPFS differs from Lustre in using distributed metadata with distributed locking rather than dedicated metadata targets, and it typically protects data with RAID or replication. Both present POSIX interfaces.

Summit's 2.5 TB/s shows the bandwidth focus. For comparison, Google says Colossus throughput regularly exceeds 50 TB/s read, but that serves many independent applications rather than a few enormous parallel jobs. Different workloads, different optimization targets.

quiz.q: Why are HPC file systems like Lustre a poor fit for web-scale warehouse and blob workloads?
quiz.a: HPC file systems are tuned for bandwidth to a few huge files and Lustre limits metadata nodes, so they can't handle billions of small files and high metadata rates.

section: Lustre and GPFS: HPC and AI training
title: AI training brought parallel file systems back into fashion
body: Large model training looks like HPC: thousands of GPUs read training data in parallel and write checkpoints at the same moment. A slow checkpoint means idle GPUs, wasting expensive compute. So AI clusters use parallel file systems or custom flash layers. Meta's 2024 GenAI clusters combine a flash-optimized Tectonic behind FUSE with Hammerspace NFS, and Meta says optimizing checkpoints cut synchronization to hundreds of milliseconds across thousands of ranks.
deeper:
Training workloads have two storage phases. Reading data is highly parallel: many GPUs each stream their share of the dataset, often repeatedly across epochs. Checkpointing is synchronized: every rank, meaning each training process, saves state at once, and the job waits until the slowest finishes. Tail latency of storage directly becomes idle time for the whole cluster.

This workload matches what Lustre and GPFS were built for: bandwidth to large files, parallel access, POSIX interfaces that frameworks already use. That is why parallel file systems, once associated mainly with supercomputers, are back in focus.

Web-scale companies have adapted their own systems as well. Meta's flash-optimized Tectonic exposes a FUSE mount so standard file code works, while flash provides the burst bandwidth. Hammerspace handles interactive developer access.

The chapter's caching section adds another piece: layers like Alluxio cache remote training data near GPUs so repeated epochs do not re-read from object storage. Together, these show AI pushing storage design back toward high-bandwidth, synchronized access patterns.

quiz.q: Why does AI training resemble HPC as a storage workload?
quiz.a: Thousands of GPUs read data in parallel and write checkpoints at the same moment; slow storage leaves all GPUs idle, so bandwidth and synchronized throughput dominate.

title: JuiceFS: a POSIX file system from a database plus an object store
body: A newer pattern puts a file system facade with caching on top of cheap, high-latency object storage. JuiceFS keeps metadata in an engine you choose, such as Redis, TiKV, MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQLite, and data in any object store. Files are split into chunks (up to 64 MB), slices and blocks (default up to 4 MB) uploaded in parallel. Clients use FUSE, a Hadoop SDK, Kubernetes CSI or an S3 gateway, with local caching.
deeper:
JuiceFS is the 'metadata in a database' idea of Colossus and Tectonic, packaged for anyone with an object store. Colossus uses Bigtable and Tectonic uses ZippyDB; JuiceFS lets you pick an existing database.

The design plays to each component's strengths. Object stores are cheap, durable and scale enormously, but they have high latency and lack file system operations like rename or directory listing with POSIX semantics. A database can answer metadata queries quickly and atomically. JuiceFS combines them: fast metadata operations from the engine, bulk data from the object store, and local caching to hide latency.

The chunk-slice-block hierarchy handles writes on immutable object storage: data is written as new blocks rather than modifying objects in place, and metadata tracks which slices make up the current file content. Parallel uploads of 4 MB blocks maximize throughput.

Multiple interfaces make it drop-in for different ecosystems: FUSE for POSIX applications, a Hadoop SDK for analytics, CSI for Kubernetes storage, and an S3 gateway. Durability, however, depends on both the object store and the metadata engine.

quiz.q: How is JuiceFS related to Colossus and Tectonic's design?
quiz.a: It applies the same 'metadata in a database' idea: metadata in a chosen engine like Redis or TiKV, data in any object store.

title: Alluxio: a caching layer that brings remote data close to compute
body: Alluxio, from UC Berkeley's AMPLab and originally called Tachyon, is a data orchestration and caching layer between compute and storage. It mounts backends like S3, GCS, HDFS, NFS, Ceph and Alibaba OSS under one namespace, and caches hot data across memory, SSD and HDD tiers. A common use is caching remote training data near GPUs, so repeated epochs of model training do not re-read everything from the object store.
deeper:
Alluxio solves a location problem. Compute and storage are often separated: GPUs in one cluster, data in a cloud object store or a remote HDFS. Every read crosses the network, adding latency and cost. Alluxio sits in between and keeps frequently used data close to the compute.

The unified namespace also simplifies access. Applications see one tree even though the underlying data may live in several different systems, similar to how HDFS ViewFs presents several namespaces as one.

Tiered caching uses each medium for what it is good at: memory for the hottest data, SSD for warm, HDD for larger cached sets.

Training workloads are ideal: each epoch reads the same dataset again. Without caching, every epoch pays the full cost of fetching from the object store; with it, the first epoch warms the cache and later epochs read locally.

The key limitation is semantic. Alluxio caches are, by design, not the source of truth. The underlying stores own durability. Alluxio adds speed and a common namespace, not durability.

quiz.q: Why does Alluxio help model training that runs many epochs over the same data?
quiz.a: The first epoch warms a cache near the GPUs, so later epochs read locally instead of re-fetching everything from a remote object store.

title: A caching layer is not your system of record
body: Common mistake: treating a caching layer as a storage system of record. JuiceFS's durability depends on both the object store and the metadata engine. If you run the metadata engine on a single Redis without persistence, you can lose the file system even though every data block is safe in S3. Alluxio caches are, by design, not the source of truth. Know which component actually owns durability before trusting a layer with data you cannot recreate.
deeper:
The JuiceFS case is subtle because the data looks safe. The object store holds every block with high durability. But blocks alone are meaningless without metadata: which blocks belong to which file, in what order, and what the directory tree looks like. If that metadata lives in a Redis instance with no persistence and it restarts, the mapping is gone, leaving an object store full of anonymous blocks.

The lesson generalizes the chapter's theme: many data outages are really metadata outages. A system's durability equals the durability of its weakest required component. For JuiceFS, the metadata engine must be as durable and replicated as the data store, for example a replicated, persistent database.

For Alluxio, the rule is simpler: it is a cache. Losing it costs performance, not data, as long as writes reach the underlying store. Problems arise when teams write data only to the cache layer or assume cached content is durable.

When evaluating any layered storage stack, trace where each piece of state lives and what protects it.

quiz.q: How can you lose a JuiceFS file system even though every data block is safe in S3?
quiz.a: If the metadata engine, like a single Redis without persistence, loses its state, the mapping from files to blocks is gone and the blocks become meaningless.

title: Metadata scaling, part 1: single master, static splits, read replicas
body: Every system in this chapter scales its data path by adding servers; they differ in how they scale metadata. The first three approaches extend a central master. A single in-memory master (GFS, early HDFS) is simple, fast and strongly consistent, but limited by RAM, CPU and recovery time. Static namespace partitioning (HDFS Federation) is an easy step up, but needs manual balancing. Read replicas of the master (HDFS Observer NameNode) offload reads, but writes still go to one node.
deeper:
Single in-memory master: all metadata in one server's RAM with an operation log. Strengths are simplicity, speed and strong semantics. Weaknesses are the three resource limits: RAM, CPU and recovery time.

Static namespace partitioning: several independent masters, each owning part of the tree, joined by ViewFs or routers. Weaknesses: manual balancing, hot directories stay hot, and cross-namespace moves are copies rather than renames.

Read replicas: followers tail the log and serve reads. Since most operations are reads, the win is big; LinkedIn and Uber both used Observer NameNodes, with LinkedIn reporting reads as about 95% of operations. Weaknesses: writes still go to one node, and a state-ID consistency protocol is needed so clients do not read stale data.

These three are incremental: each keeps the familiar single-master code and adds capacity around it. They are the natural path for an existing system, which is why HDFS took it. They postpone the ceiling rather than removing it, because write throughput and per-namespace memory remain bound to single processes.

quiz.q: Why are read replicas of the metadata master such a big win, and what limit remains?
quiz.a: Most metadata operations are reads, so followers can absorb most load; but all writes still go to one node and a state-ID protocol is needed for consistency.

title: Metadata scaling, part 2: databases, layers, formulas and subtrees
body: The remaining approaches restructure metadata. Metadata in a distributed database (Colossus on Bigtable, Tectonic on ZippyDB, JuiceFS) scales to billions of files, but cross-shard operations like rename are hard. Layered metadata by kind (Tectonic, ADLS, Azure) scales each layer separately, with more RPC hops. Computed placement (Ceph CRUSH) needs no location table, but data moves when the map changes. Big units with a small index elsewhere (Azure stream layer) keep bottom metadata tiny. Subtree partitioning (CephFS, Lustre DNE) keeps directory locality.
deeper:
Details per approach:

Distributed database: the namespace and block maps are rows in a sharded database. Strength: billions of files and exabytes. Weakness: cross-shard operations like rename are hard, and the system depends on the database.

Layered by kind: separate layers for names, files and blocks, or extents versus objects. Tectonic hash-partitions, ADLS range-partitions, Azure splits stream and partition layers. Strength: each layer scales and caches separately. Weakness: more moving parts and RPC hops.

Computed placement: a function maps objects to disks. Strength: no block-location table. Weakness: data moves when the map changes; less control per object.

Big units, small index elsewhere: track 1 GB extents, index objects in another layer. Strength: tiny metadata at the bottom. Weakness: needs a second scalable index layer.

Subtree partitioning: metadata servers own parts of the directory tree and rebalance. Strength: locality for directory operations. Weakness: balancing is hard and subtrees can get hot.

Real systems combine these: Tectonic is both database-backed and layered; Ceph pairs CRUSH with subtree-partitioned MDS.

quiz.q: What is the typical weakness of putting file system metadata in a distributed database?
quiz.a: Cross-shard operations such as rename become hard, and the file system depends on the database's availability and behavior.

title: Review a storage design by finding its metadata path first
body: Senior staff lens: when you review a storage design, find the metadata path first. Ask how many metadata objects there are per PB. Ask what the read/write ratio of metadata operations is. Ask which operations are cross-shard: rename, listing a huge directory, deleting a tree. Ask how long metadata recovery takes after a crash. Many 'data' outages are really metadata outages: the bytes are safe, but nobody can find them.
deeper:
Each question maps to a lesson in the chapter.

Objects per PB: HDFS's rule of about 1 GB of NameNode metadata per PB assumes average file sizes; small files multiply the object count. LinkedIn and Uber hit namespace limits before disks filled.

Read/write ratio: LinkedIn saw reads at about 95% of NameNode operations, which made Observer NameNodes a big win. A write-heavy metadata workload would not benefit the same way.

Cross-shard operations: in a hash-partitioned or database-backed design, a rename or recursive delete touches many shards and becomes expensive or non-atomic. Knowing which operations users rely on tells you whether the partitioning scheme fits.

Recovery time: GFS writes stopped while the master loaded its checkpoint and replayed its log. HDFS standbys must read all edits before becoming active.

The outage point ties it together: JuiceFS with a non-persistent Redis loses the file system while data blocks survive in S3. Durability and availability are only as good as the metadata path.

quiz.q: Why does the read/write ratio of metadata operations matter when reviewing a storage design?
quiz.a: It decides which scaling approach helps: read-heavy metadata benefits greatly from read replicas like Observer NameNodes, while write-heavy metadata needs a partitioned or distributed design.

title: Ten file systems side by side: units, redundancy and consistency
body: Comparing the systems: GFS (2003) used 64 MB chunks, 3x replication and relaxed consistency. Colossus uses client-encoded stripes with replication and Reed-Solomon; its consistency model is not fully published. HDFS uses 128 MB blocks, 3x rack-aware or striped EC, single writer. Tectonic uses per-tenant encoding and linearizable metadata. Azure's stream layer uses 1 GB extents, 3x then LRC(12,2,2), strong consistency. Ceph offers replication or EC pools, strong in RADOS. Lustre and GPFS are POSIX. JuiceFS and Alluxio delegate redundancy to backends.
deeper:
Published scale anchors each system: GFS 1,000+ nodes and 300+ TB (2003); Colossus two file systems over 10 EB each (2025); HDFS at LinkedIn 500 PB in one cluster and 1 EB total (2021); Tectonic a 1,590 PB cluster with 10.7B files (2021); Azure 70 PB raw (2011) with stamps up to 30 PB; Ceph at many PB-scale users like CERN and DigitalOcean; Lustre 679 PB Orion at Frontier; GPFS 250 PB and 2.5 TB/s at Summit.

Interfaces split into two families. Custom or append-only APIs (GFS, Colossus, Tectonic, Azure streams, HDFS write-once) give up POSIX to simplify replication and scale. POSIX systems (Lustre, GPFS, and JuiceFS and Alluxio as options) serve applications that expect standard file semantics.

Redundancy shows a clear trend from 3x replication toward erasure coding, often applied after data is sealed. Lustre typically relies on hardware RAID under OSTs rather than cross-server redundancy.

Metadata design is the distinguishing column: RAM master, database, layered, computed, or delegated. Unit of storage ranges from 4 MB JuiceFS blocks to 1 GB Azure extents.

quiz.q: Which systems in the comparison give up POSIX semantics, and why?
quiz.a: GFS, Colossus, Tectonic, Azure streams and HDFS use custom append-only or write-once APIs, trading POSIX for simpler replication, encoding and scale.

title: Chapter recap: each DFS is a new answer to metadata scaling
body: The data path scales easily; the metadata path does not, and each DFS generation is a new answer. GFS chose one in-memory master, 64 MB chunks, leases and relaxed consistency; the master became the limit. Colossus moved metadata into Bigtable behind curators and scales over 100x past GFS. HDFS copied GFS, then added federation, QJM HA, observers and EC. Tectonic replaced Haystack, f4 and HDFS with hash-partitioned layered metadata. Azure tracks 1 GB extents. Ceph computes placement.
deeper:
The remaining takeaways fill in the picture.

HDFS limits are NameNode RAM, about 600 bytes per average file, and RPC load, yet LinkedIn runs 500 PB in one cluster with about 1 billion objects on one NameNode (2021).

Tectonic's metadata is split into Name, File and Block layers on ZippyDB, and each tenant chooses its own encoding.

Azure's stream layer keeps metadata small by tracking 1 GB extents, seals them, and erasure codes them with LRC; the object index lives in the partition layer.

Ceph's CRUSH removes block-location metadata but makes data move when the cluster map changes. BlueStore showed that building on local file systems can cost more than it saves.

Lustre and GPFS dominate HPC and are back in focus for AI training because of parallel reads and synchronized checkpoints.

JuiceFS and Alluxio add file semantics and caching over object storage; JuiceFS durability depends on the metadata engine too.

Two Colossus file systems exceed 10 EB each as of 2025.

quiz.q: What single idea connects all the systems in this chapter?
quiz.a: The data path scales by adding servers; each system is a different answer to scaling the metadata path.
